WHITE ROSE.
By GERALD RISS.
CHAPTER XXVII.

Wrruier a few minutes after mindight ati the conspirators had all gathered in the ban- queting-hall at Hampstead House. All looked anxious, and one or two of the faces appeared positively haggard in the white light. As soon as the preliminaries had been transacted, Otto rose from his seat. "Ladies and gentlemen," he said in his clear, resonant voice, "we have been obliged to call an emergency meeting to-night owing to an untoward circumstance, which may endanger the whole cause. But, before call- ing upon Lord Branksca to report, I have one piece of encouraging news to announce. To- day the Earl of Fulford offered the Secretary- ship of State for War to the Marquis of Swanage in place of Lord Oddingly." Those round the table broke into delighted applause at this unexpected piece of good news. " Nothing could be more timely or fortunate, and it will be of inestimable advantage to the cause. At my personal request he has decided to accept the position." Again there was applause. " Now," concluded Otto sternly, " I cal! upon Lord Branksea to report." Branksea rose, pale and nervous, and, as he stood, he gripped the table for support. "Your Majesty," he said, speaking halt- ingly, "I left here last night, as arranged, with the Earl of Ben Nevis and had mode up my mind to follow in exact detail the success- ful plan adopted by the Earl of Portcullis in the case of Lord Oddingi.v. I stopped the car exactly as he did and kited the bonnet under the pretence of making an examination of the engine. Then I called out to Ben Nevis to come and look, but I got no answer. When I withdrew my head, there was no sign ot nitn anywhere! He had not appeared to be sus- picious of rue in any way, and it came as a complete surprise ,to me. But the fact re- mained that he had bolted across the heath, where I could not follow him on the car. I was at my wits' end to know what to do for a time, and then I decided to drive straight down west, garage the car, and lie in wait for him in Half Moon Street. There was the Chance of his making straight for Scotland Yard or even the nearest police-station, but I had no option but to risk that. The only place where I had any likelihood of catching him was at his own chambers. So I.- went to Half Moon Street and waited, huddled up on a doorstep in the shadow of a portico. It seemed hours and hours before he came, and it was terribly cold. I was almost frozen," he went on pathetically, "and could hardly grasp the knife, and that is, I suppose, how I came to bungle the business. And then, on top of everything, a policeman appeared round the corner, and I had to run for my life. I got away safely and, gentlemen," he concluded bitterly, " you know the rest." He sat down wearily and buried his face in his hands. Then Otto rose and spoke. "Lord Branksea," he said, "I should be the last to doubt your devotion to the cause or to question your earnest endeavour tc carry out the duty that fell to you, but, on the other hand, by your failure you have not only endangered the ultimate success of our aims, but the lives of all present." A shiver passed over Branksea, and he murmured something inaudibly, as Otto sat down. "I should suggest, if I may be allowed to do so, your Majesty," he said in his cool voice, "that, as reparation for his failure, Lord Brank- sea should be deputed to make another effort to complete his task. If he succeeds and gets away, well and good. If he is, on the other hand, taken flagrante delicto, he must pose as a homicidal maniac and take upon his shoulders the blame of the whole affair, throwing the police off the track." " near, hear," came from all round the table, as Carruthers resumed his seat. - Lord Portcullis, bloodshot and unsteady, followed. "He should have killed policeman, too, instead of running away. He would have saved the whole situation if he had only done 50.,.

One after another spoke, all agreeing that the only hope left was to make another at- tempt upon Ben Nevis's life. " He is not expected to live, as it is," said Sir Andrew Wentworth, bringing his expert knowledge to bear on the subject. " Sholto,

who is in charge of the case, told me that the S. heart has actually been pierced. but that he has sewn it up. Of course, there is r. slight chance of recovery, and there are precedents; but it is unlikely. The least violence,, any- thing that would disturb the stitches _would be fatal. Lord Ben Nevis is further suffeling from concussion from the fall, so his state is even more critical, as he is likely to become delirious and may thus injure himself." The statement of the fashionable physician was listened to with the utmost interest. Then Otto spoke again, addressing Brank- sea. "Are you willing to undertake this danger- ous attempt, Lord Branksea? I feel that it is only fair to others that you should do so ; but, at the same time, it is a very forlorn hope, full of danger to yourself." Branksea's black eyes glittered. He was no coward ; and the announcement of Ben Nevis's engagement by the evening papers had only served to intensify his hatred. He rose from his seat, drawing a latch-key from his pocket. "I am ready, your Majesty," he said, speaking with more confidence, "to under- take what I feel to be my duty to all present." He was interrupted by applause. Then he resumed : "More by chance than anything else, last night I picked up Ben Nevis's latch-key which fell out of his hand, when I was stoop- ing down in an attempt to put the white rose into his button-hole. So I have an unexpected means of entry into the house, and I shall lay my plans carefully." Frazer rose to speak. "I know Ben Nevis's rooms, and may, perhaps, be allowed to offer a suggestion as to a plan of campaign. In the passage then, are heavy plush curtains, in which a man ....could easily conceal himself without people passing to and fro being any the wiser. His rooms consist of a sitting-room in front and a bed- room behind, separated by folding door. Each room has its own door into the passage. When I was calling this afternoon„ I learnt by casual inquiry that Lady Grizelle Belsize has taken the vacant drawing-room floor for the present. Now it seems to me that once in the passage and hidden in the curtain, Lord Branksea can await his opportunity. If he slips into the house somewhere near dinner- time, when they all go off upstairs to dinner, and the patient is left alone with the nurse. then would be the time to strike. Of course, if the nurse interferes, or is in the way, so much the worse for the nurse I" After a prolonged discussion it was finally arranged that Branksea should make another effort the following evening, and, forlorn hope that it was, it seemed to lighten the anxiety of the conspirators. The Duke Of Hampstead had been most noticeably quiet the whole evening, and not a word had passed his lips during the discussion up on the second attempt on Ben Nevis's life. That concluded, he rose to speak. " Your Majesty, ladies and gentlemen," he said in a quick, nervous way, "I must first assure you that what I am about to say is not in any way influenced by the statement that Lord Ben Nevis is engaged to my daughter. On the contrary, I deny that he is, and recog- nise no such state of affairs. I have, there- fore, left you to discuss and decide upon the /natter without interfering with or interrupt- t.o,;,, your arrangements. What is best for the cause must be done at all costs. But I must admit that I am sick, heartily sick of this bloodshed, and am desirous of putting an end to it as far as possible. Hence the plan which I am about to unfold to you, which will bring matters more peaceably to a head. I have already laid the scheme before his

div.head: McDOUGALUS Pategt SELF-RAISING FLOUR BDRIVIEw. The Examiner, Saturday, November 25, 1905. '
div.p: McDOUGALUS Pategt SELF-RAISING FLOUR BDRIVIEw. The Examiner, Saturday, November 25, 1905. '

Majesty. who has given it 1219 tuuest ap- proval." Otto nodded affirmatively. "The plan," continued the daze, "is timply this, and simplicity itself. It is merely to kidnap the reigning King and hold him up to ransom on our own terms, forcing him to abdicate peacefully in favour of King Charles III."
Everybody sat up suddenly, listening with wrapt attention, and the sensation caused by the duke's own words was obvious.

"The King—l use the title as one of convenience—as you are all aware, is spending this coming week-end at Southsea Castle. as the guest of the duchess and myself; and, though it goes very much against the grain to violate any of the established canons of hospitality, I feel that it is an opportunity not to be lost upon any amount, especially as it may lead to a more p.,..eeful solution of the problem before us. I have a small secluded house right in the heart oil the New Forest a few miles. from the Castle. It has not been occupied for some years, but has always been kept in good repair and has only lately been overhauled. There even the King might be concealed for any length of time without suspicion being aroused, though the whole country would be in an uproar with regard to his disappearance, and it would be perfectly easy to arrange to kidnap him. I have a new type of motor-car, which the King has expressed his eagerness to try. He shell go for a run upon it, driven by Lord Bra.nksea or Mr. Gordon, who could suggest taking him to .see this interesting old dower-house. There they would find two others waiting—the Master of Gareloch and Sir Alan Atherley. When the king enters a certain room, which has been pre- pared on the lines of a padded chamber, yet thoroughly comfortable for occupation, -sem be MT easiest thing in the world to turn the key and slip the bolts. The house is being well 'provisioned, and a plentiful stock of wine and cigars is being sent to make things as comfortable as possible. Mrs. Anderson, the wife of the gate-keeper here, will act as cook and housekeeper. The motor will be found miles away, somewhere near the seashore, and whoever is driving it will simply disappear, too. This plan seems to me sim- plicity itself, and it is I, outside, who will have to stand the racket of public criticism, but, for- tunately. I can afford to do so in my position. If the King is only amenable to reason it will greatly strengthen our hand. PossiVy it may save all further bloodshed, which is the chief thing to be desired." The duke resumed his seat brushing back his hair wearily, and an outbreak of applause followed. Member after member of the committee spoke, each praising the simplicity of the scheme and offering to do their share, and, in conclusion, Otto added his approval to the general verdict. " Well, then," said the duke, "that is) all settled, and, in consultation with his Majesty and Mr. Frazer, I will complete all the details of the scheme. Sunday, it seems to me, would be the moot suitable day. But the thing in the forefront of our programme is Lord Branksca's attempt to complete his task."
"I will do my best," said Branksea, rising and bdwing to Otto; " I will act to-morrow evening."
CHAPTER XXVIII.

THE following afternoon Branksea called al Half Moon Street, ostensibly to inquire aftet Ben Nevis. This, he decided, was the sim- plest way in which to spy out the land. In response to his ring the door was opened by the landlord, who motioned to Branksea to speak softly. Seeing his opportunity, he stepped inside and gave the inPsi his card. "I have called to inquire after Lord Ben Nevis," he said almost in a whisper. Mean- while, his black eyes were roving round the narrow hall, noting all the details of the furniture.

The ground-floor rooms which Ben Nevis occupied lay to the left beyond heavy plush curtains, which were drawn to preclude any sound. The left-hand side of the hall itself was bare, except for a couple of pictures and a trophy of Zulus' shields and spears. On the right-hand side stood a tall hat-stand, flanked by two chairs. The further chair almost touched the curtains which were very full and had obviously decorated some more imposing place before finding themselves in such straitened circumstances.

Branksea felt satisfied at the result pf ht survey. It would be easy enough to secrete himself behind the voluminous folds of the curtain in such a way that it would not be noticeable, should anybody pass through the hall, which was only lit by a single gas-lamp hung high owing. to the height of the ceiling.

"Lori Ben Nevis is mirch the same, my lord, thank you," the man told him in the meantime, " neither better nor worse as far as the doctors can tell. His lordship has not yet recovered consciousness, and they fear, when he does, he'll be delirious. The doctors have sewed up the heart, but are afraid of any movement at present." " Thank you," said Braid:sea, the main object of his curiosity satisfied. "I am glad to hear such comparatively good news. Who is with him ? "

"Lady Sabina Belsize will hardly leave him day or night, my lord," answered the man "and, of course, there are two nurses to help her, I.ady Grizelle Charteris has taken all the rest of the house, and is living on the drawing-room floor, where they take their meals, and Lady Sabina's maid is here, too." "You might give Lady Sabina my card later on," said Branksea, having gained all the information he wanted, "and tell her how grieved I am not to hear better news. Good day." Good day, my lord, and thank you," re- plied the old soldier, as Branksea left the house. "I will give her ladyship your message." _ .

Branksea felt decidedly relieved at the result of his survey, as things looked more promising than he had anticipated. " VII do for him yet," he muttered to himself almost cheerfully-, "it it's to be managed. Apart from everything, he has come between Bina and me. The best time will he about dinner-time, when they are upstairs, all except the nurse. I'll slip into the house about half- past seven and wait my opportunity." Knowing the necessity of showing up at the club, he made his way round to the Un- attached, where he surprised everybody by his unusual geniality of manner. " Poor Ben Nevis," he said ; "I've jist been round to leave cards. and inquire, and I'm glad to say that he is going oil as well as possible. Interesting case, the doctors say." And he proceeded to dilate upon .it for the benefit of his audience.

"The heart was actually pierced, and they've had to sew it up, the old chap at the door told me. It's a thing they've done successfully before now, but, of course, it's a ticklish job. If he gets delirious and moves, the stitches are liable to break, and then he'll be done for. But he's Still unconscious from the concussion, and they hope it will be all right." Branksea ordered himself a whisky and soda. He felt he deserved one.
Then the conversation became general. . Soon after five he got up. " Well,.you chaps, I must be off. See you later."
He signed to Atherley to follow him, and the latter rose.' •

" Everything is arranged," he said in a low voice in the hall. "'I try'ragain to-night about eight o'clock. I want you to be wait- ing for me at that time with a. motor in Curzon Street just round the corner." Atherley nodded. "I'll be there," he answered, "and ready to start."

Branksea left the club and called a cab, in which he drove round to Swanage House. Carefully avoiding the chance of meeting anyone, he went straight up to his dressing- room and slipped off his frock-coat and outer clothes. From his wardrobe he selected a dark tweed suit of a nondescript Pattern, a muffler

for his neck, a large motor cap, which he could pull right down over his ears and fore- head, and a pair of tan tennis shoes with rubber soles. Into his pocket he slipped a pair of motor-goggles. He chuckled to himself as he made his pre- parations, congratulating himselt on tus perspicuity. "1 shall look like an anarchist 'when I'm made up," he muttered, " and I'm sure no onc will recognisee me. Then he opened a drawer which was locke6 a white rose.
and took out the knife he had used before and " I'll leave it, if I get a chance, just to show them," he thought vindictively. "It will give them something to talk about?'

He left the house quietly and walked a little way before he picked up a cab. "Drive to Morton's," he said, mention- ing the name of a well-known costumier. He entered the shop boldly and I utton- holed one of the assistants.

" I want to be made up at once," he said with a smil; "something between a foreign chauffeur and an anarchist. The truth is," he went on confidentially, "I want to play a practical jokc on a lady and don't want her tc recognise. me."

Tlie man laughed. " All right, sir ; we'll manage that for you." He took him into a private room and set to work, combing his brushed up moustache down over his mouth and adding a shaggy beard. Then he added a few finishing touches.
Looking in the glass Dranksea was sur- prised at the change in his appearance. "Delicious," he exclaimed with a laugh. "What a ruffian I look ! "

Then he paid the man, tipping him hand- somely and left the shop. Seeing that it was nearly half-past seven he took a cab and drove to Curzon Street, where he got out. Then, making a slight detour, he doubled on his tracks and found himself at the north end of Half Moon Street. Hardly a soul was in sight, as he drew near the house. He noticed a light in the sitting-room and one on the floor above, but the hall was in dark- ness.

Quickly and noiselessly he put the latchkey in the lock and turned it. It was a nervous moment, as he felt that his chief danger was the possibility of meeting someone actually in the hall. As swiftly as possible he slipped inside and closed it without a sound. It had only taken a second; but it had been an

into the inner hail, pausing a seconct to accustom his eyes to the light. He moved softly forward towards the second door, and with a firm grip turned the handle noi,elesslv, stepping swiftly aside. It was almost' dark in the room, only a shaded lamp burning in the corner, and most of the light came from the front room through the folding doors, which were partially open< The bed was in the far corner hidden behind the open door, and Eranksea saw that he would have to cross the zone of light to reach it. Nerving himself for the final ordeal, he stepped forward with the knife in his right hand, intending to cross the band of light with a single stride. Then a strange thing happened. As he advanced the door moved' toward him, as though being closed by some unseen agency; and behind it he raw Bina just leaving the bedside with a cup in 'ler hand. She saw him just as he saw her ; and both started back, the girl uttering a sharp cry. Then, almbst mechanically, she raised the cup and dashed its hot contents into his face, blinding him for an instant. At the same time he heard a growl and a 3narl, and he felt a dog's teeth meet in his leg. With an oath he jumped back, slashing ai Mike with the knife, till the dog released his grip. Then his over-strained nerve gave way, and he turned and fled, dashing through the darb hall and slamming the door behind him. In the sick-room Mike lay still, the latest victim of the "White Rose,' and, as a token, the white rose intended for Bell Nevis lay beside his body in a pool of bloc d. . ITo be continued.)

ULTRA-MICROSCOPIC PARASITES. In certain important groups of microbic dis- eases, the parasites causing them are unknown— that is to say, no parasites can be detected by the microscope or by culture—but it is equally true, says Popular Seicnrc Siftings, that they must be present in the blood and fluids of the sick animals in some form or other. In all pro. bability they are ultra-microscopic—too small to be seen with our present instruments. This is borne out by the fact that they are able to pass through the pores of porcelain filters, which keep back the smallest micro-organisms we are able to recognise.

div.head: INGENIOUS ANTS.
div.p: INGENIOUS ANTS.

Certain observations made by Mr. W. M. Wheeler may, it is thought, throw some light on the origin of the curious slave-making habits of certain ants. Females of one species (Formica difficilis have been seen to enter singly colonies of anpther species (F. schaufussi), which had no queens of their own. The progeny of these alien queens is duly fed and reared by the workers of the invaded colonies. In time the workers die off, leaving a colony of foreigners. Suppose, however, that before the original workers die off the new corners make raids, and capture more to supplyi their place, then an ordi- nary case of slavery s the result. _
ALUMINIUM AND MERCURY FUMES.

Workers in mercury mines, and in works where this metal is used, run the danger of breathing injurious mercurial vapours. The re- markable property possessed by the metal alu- minium of completely absorbing such vapours, even when they are largely mixed with air, has been made the basis of a very Olt ient respirator for those who incur any risk of poi.soiring in this way. The inhaled air, i s made to pass through a mass of finely divided aluminium, and during this passage every trace of mercury vapour is absorbed. Air contaminated even with dense fumes of mercury can thus be breathed with impunity. The respirator has been used in the mercury mines of Monte Amiata in Italy with good results.

THE GLOW OF THE SHOOTING STAR. a The generally given explanation of the glow a the shooting star is that the stony or metallic mass becomes heated to incandescence by friction in its rapid passage through the air. Professor A. S. Herschel, however, points out that this is a mistake. The glow is in reality produced by a swirl of incandescent air, which forms the meteor's head, and this is due to the heat developed by the compression of the air in front by the meteor's rapid motion. If a meteor is moving at the rate of thirty miles a second, the calculated temperature of the air in front works out to 1,180,620 deg. C. The air remains a per- fectly elastic and frictionlesas fluid in spite of the enormous velocity of the meteor passing through it.

div.head: CORALS OFF IRELAND.
div.p: CORALS OFF IRELAND.

The recent discovery of a coral, belonging to the same family as the precious coral of com- merce, off the West Coast of Ireland, is of special scientific interest. Hitherto this family has only been obtained from the Mediterranean, the seas round Japan, Madeira, Cape de Verde Island, and the Bamda •Sea. The species was obtained by the fisheries branch of the Department of Agriculture in 382 fathoms, sixty miles off the island of Achil. Pieurocoral- hum Johnsoni, as the Irish coral is named, is not itself of commercial value, though nearly re-- lated to the precious kinds. Some of the most valuable coral obtained in the Japanese fisheries, for example, is supplied by the species pleuro- corallium elatium. And since in these and other fisheries the valuable and worthless species of coral occur together, it is suggested that pre- cious corals also may exist off the Irish coast. Three other species of • coral, and three related genera, have also been obtained, the former belonging to a group not hitherto found in Irish waters.

div.head: THEORY' OF GLACIATION.
div.p: THE THEORY' OF GLACIATION.

According to the astronomical theory ot glaci- ation set forth by Dr. Croll, the cold period in one hemisphere was simultaneous with a warm period in the other. Now, according to a large number of observations, 'glaciation is at present diminishing in Arctic regions. Hence, according to the above theory, it ought to be increasing in the Antarctic. Facts collected by the Discovery, under Captain Scott, however, shew that the contrary is the case. The glaciatiOn of the Ant- arctic is also diminishing. During the two sum- mers of Sir James Ross's visit the slopes of Mount Terror' remained covered with snow. Captain Scott, however, found bare land over large areas of the mountain. This is only one of many indichtions of a lessening of glaciation. Yet the climatic conditions of the Antarctic are probably not less, but rather more, severe. The lessening glaciation, in fact, is duo to the smaller snowfall. And it was this small snow- fall that enabled Captain Scott to travel 300 miles over the ice towards the south without see- ing any signs of an end. Thus the present cli- matic conditions of the Polar regions do not lend support to the astronomical theory of glaciation.

div.head: BOMBS FOR HAIL:
div.p: BOMBS FOR HAIL:

In a note presented to the Acad6mie des Sciences; M. Vidal shows the efficacy of the hail- destroying bombs which he has invented. On one occasion, he says, a severe storm which was con- densed on the highest summits of the Bernese Alps at altitudes above 10,000 ft came down through the narrow valley of the Rhone. All the localities were much damaged by hail, except the places where the bombs. were fired into the air, and this seems to be a good proof as to the efficacy of this means of preventing hail. Be- sides this, M. Vidal brings out a point in mete- orology discovered during the storm, and hither- to completely unobserved. The clouds seemed to have been banked in, and were only allowed to follow a certain path. It is remarked that all the localities which lay higher than 2,200 ft. alti- tude escaped damage by the storm. We thus have a valuable indication as to the height of the storm-clouds, and it seems certain that they kept at a very short distance from the ground. ilt s due to the low altitude that the rockets and bombs against the hail are so effective. They are easily fired, and explode in the air at 1,2001 t. or 1,500 ft. altitude. M. Vidal proposes the study of the map so as to find the habitual paths of storms, then ito place advance guard posts which protect a certain region by firing the bombs and prevent the rain from changing to hail. The question of protection against storms is a scien- tific problem, and the official observatories could greatly aid in the solution, which is so important in the agricultural districts.

div.head: EXCITING STRUGGLE IN A TRAIN. Determined Suicide Near Warrington
div.p: EXCITING STRUGGLE IN A TRAIN. Determined Suicide Near Warrington

A verdict of "Suicide whilst of unsound mind "was returned by a Warrington jury on Tuesday at an inquest which was held on the body of John Cooksoon (401) of 14. Portland-street, Lancaster, who died from self- inflicted wounds, at the Warrington Infirmary on Satur- day. Deceased who was employed asa grocers salesman by Messrs. T: D. Smith Ltd., Lancaster, had suffered from fits of depression for a long time and on Friday cut his throat while travelling with his brother on the railway between Wigan and Warrington. At the Inquest on Tuesday, William Cookson, clerk 49, Ellesmere-road, said that owing to a communication from his brother's employers he, on Monday 17th visited Lancaster in order to bring him back to Warrington and have him medically examined. They left Lancaster by the 5.25 p.m. train and all went well until Preston was reached. He noticed his brother was in a very bad state of nervousness and having to make some enqhiries with regard to the journey he left him in charge of two railway officials to whom he explained his situation. From Preston to Wigan they were accompanied by a railway detective. Leaving Wigan they travelled alone in a first class compartment. His t brother -pulled out a pocket knife and commenced ' cleaning his finger nails. Witness asked deceased to lend him the knife and John at Once gave it to him. Deceased immediately pulled out of his pocket a larger knife and before witness could prevent it plunged the Iblade into his throat. Witness at once seized him I and a terrible struggle ensued, and it was not until his hands bad been badly cut that he obtained possession of the knife. With difficulty he pulled the communica- tion cord,and the train stopped at Winwick Quay where he got the assistance of an ambulance man, who dressed his brother's wound. The journey was continued to Warrington, where the deceased was conveyed to the Infirmary. Mr. Hatton, who appeared on behalf of the relatives of the deceased, said that Mr. Smith, head of the firm of Messrs. T. D. Smith, Ltd., had come from Lancaster to give evidence as to his observations of the deceased's mental condition, and also as to the fact that there was absolutely nothing wrong financially, and that the rela- tions between the deceased and his employers was of the most cordial kind. - _
--- Edward Garrill Smith, of the firm of Messrs. T. D. Smith, Ltd., supported this statement. Mr. Brighouse : There was no financial trouble at all?

Witness : On the contrary last week with a view to cheer him up we had a most encouraging report of a recenting stock-taking to give him. The jury in returning the above verdict expressed their sympathy with the relatives of the deceased.

div.p: THE SERF'S PROGRESS.

The following letter appeared in the" Daily News on Wednesday: Sir,—.By cable you report that yester- day the British Government in the Transvaal hanged , four slaves for murder. These men had escaped from the compounds, possibly to avoid brutal treatment. Having escaped, they became outlaws. No man darer give them shelter or work, for to do so would be to. • subject himself to tine or imprisonment under the terms of the Chinese Labour Ordinance. These fugitive' - slaves were starving, and attempted to rob a farmstead. •-• The Dutchman defended his property. and the serfs v. killed him. And yesterday the British Government& hanged them* Yet another "regrettable necessity,"— Yours, etc.,
R. L. OUTTIWAITE.

PLANT POISONS. • The question of the action of poisons in dif. ferent plants has been examined by G. J. Stracke, a German scientist. We observe, says the Scientific „American, that a great number of plants show toxic secretions or excretions, but still continue to live, in spite of the poisonous matter which they contain. It is possible that the plant is protected by localising the poison in some of the tissues or in determined cells, which are thus sacrificed, and that thick walls serve to isolate the dangerous regions from the other parts, but, on the other hand, it is certain that proto-vegetable matter can exist in contact with the poisons of some bodies without being destroyed. M. Stracke makes some researches which are interesting, even though incomplete. He determines the resistance of ' a vegetable ti,..,;ue to solutions of different poisons, according to the degree of plasrnolysis and sometimes by a change of colour which follows the .death of the grten tissue. div.head: PADGAT E.
div.p: PADGAT E.

WESi/EY GUILD.—A successful meeting of the Padgate Wesley Guild was held on Monday at which there was a large attendance. A lecture "An evening with Dr- Johnson," was delivered by the Rev. John Gunnell, over which the Rev. W. Mellor presided. The lecturer drew a very vivid picture of the life of the great lexicographer giving an excellent description of his early life, his poverty and struggles of his wonderful memory and marvellous power of acquiring knowledge; his friendship with Burke, Garrick and especially with Boswell--the writer of his life. He noted the fact that to-day Irving had just been laid to rest in Westminster Abbey in close proximity to the spot where lay the ashes of Garrick and Johnson. He also instanced the great conversa- tional powers of the sage and his large-hearted generosity. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. IGlnnnell on the motion of Messrs. Leonard Bennett and Ernest Haigh, supported by Mr. F. Wright.

div.head: HUMOUR AMONG THE FISHER-FOLK,
div.p: HUMOUR AMONG THE FISHER-FOLK,
- ATHOL FORBES Author of Came*. and Comedy," "4 Son of Innmon," " Odd _Fish," te.)

" It's all through that there arrow, sir, on the Church Tower." I had heard many surpris- ing explanations of things from my old salt-water friend, Cutting, but the arrow on the church tower as a reason for entering the holy state of matrimony rather staggered me. Cupid's Arrow of course—but the wind vane on the church flagstaff—" How do you mean i" I asked. ` Yea, you may look, sir, but its right. The arrow has done the trick—put in the banns if you please. It is a curryus thing, sir," he con- tinued, " but I ain't seen that there arrow for nigh on forty year. Yis'day I seed it quite plain like, just as L used to see it when I was a boy. Yes, you caii put in the banns, for I'm going to marry Ann King. She's a dainty craft, saucy, and sixty-seven, she's good for some years yet. Why them new teeth she got the other day cost nigh ten pounds, so they tell me. Oh, she's in pod repair." " How old are you, Cutting ?" I enquired. " Eighty-five this spring fishing," he replied.. " But as say I can see that there arrow quite plain. and I can see to look after another ship— meanin' thereby a wife. Why, sir, I feel quite young again—a mere boy. Why, what is it, sir I" _ .
I was lying back in my :chair laughing as the explanation of the arrow as the factor in de- termining old Cutting's decision burst, uptin me.
A CI:ILE FOR NAILING VISION.

We bad just placed a new wind indicator—a huge gilded arrow on the top of the ehurch tower flagstaff. The old one afler a useful life of two hundred and odd years disappeared one night in a gale of wind. The new one was three times the length of the old, and eorre,pond- ingly large, thus it was that old Cutting saw it plainly. He had not beard of the dill'erence in size, hence the inference that his eyesight had " come agiu," as be described it. It was a ease of healthy suggestion acting npon his whole constitution, and he felt better all round. Cutting was not the only one whose general health improved with better vision. `c'everal old-life boatmen, and a couple of supenainuated pilots found they could see that arrow quite clearly now. "it means rain WhCll you enn see tut clear as that," said Captain- Leggott. " its -due to the clear atmosphere—everything gettin' out o' the way o' the wet. You see the air is full o' parasites of all kinds, and rain water kills 'em."

"I'll tell you lads what it is, it's a mirage. I've seen them to the Suth'ard o' the line," was another old skipper's theory—" Au it be- longs to the sooper-natral." such was the conversation on the pier when the new arrow of twelve feet instead of four was first lloticed. The difference in size has remained a secret until now. The subject of marriage naturally suggests courtship. Fisher- men have a great respect for women. Perhaps it is because they do not see so much of them as the ordinary landsman—at least this has been suggested as an explanation. He is always polite to them. " No, lady," " Yes, lady," and a quick readiness to ,be of service to what has been termed "the sex,?' are alike indicative of his courtesy and his gallantry. - " Has boy , George been to see you this morning, sir ?" And a briglit'tdark-eyed hailed me from a cottage window not long ago. " Yes," I replied. " Ile chucked his sou-'ester in last night," and she laughed merrily. . . .

And that was his proposal of marriage—it done without a word. The young lover, or old for that matter, will open the door of the cot- tage, whcre dwells the maiden of his choice, and simply throw in his head gear. If there be more daughters than one, it is accompanied by the name of her who has won his heart. Shanhl ,the sou'-wester be allowed to remain he follows it into the house. If his addressee are unwel- come it is promptly thrown out, and the disap- pointed' swain goes off without more ado. If tho lady - later on repent her decision the ad- vance must come from her, and she has many ways of doing it.

div.head: TURN 'EKE OTHER CREEK.
div.p: TURN 'EKE OTHER CREEK.

"Why, Rose," I said to a girl, who came to put in the banns, " James told me last week that you had refused him." " Yes, sir, but I thought better of it, so last night on the pier I just went up to him and smacked his face." Then Jim chased her— caught her and kissed her for it, and in order to keep her in better order bound her " to love, honour and obey " him in the future as his law- ful wife. It-•••ezill be seen that a smack in the face is in some instances a mark of affection, and sign of encouragement. No doubt it is a relic of the days when man was ever the mighty hunter, and courting was a more serious busi- ness than it is nciw, and the claws of the bride made their final protest against self surrender. A little knowledge is a dangerous thing, and, it is fatal to air that little hi the presence ofi experts. A bishop, who shall be muueless, was spending a few days with me, and as he has more adaptability than, the majority of his bre- thren on the bench, he was soon friends with the fishermen he met. " Well, and what have you been doing f" he asked of a little group on the pier head, by way of making conversation. "Well, as 'a matter of fact, your reverence, we have just been splicing the main brace.' " They laughed good humouredly, and I smiled; the bishop looked grave, then remarked: " Well, I hope you made a good job of it." This pleased the men, and on the spot I could see they voted him a good sort. It never dawned on me that my episcopal superior was unaware of the meaning of the phrase, and as I there may be others equally ignorant, I may any " splice the main brace" means, have a drink.

div.head: AWILLING CREW,
div.p: AWILLING CREW,

The next scene in this little comedy is the Parish Church. and a large gathering of fisher- men are there to hear the bishop preach. His subject was "Courage,' and he handled it well. To my horror in a very impressive part of his discourse he said, "If at the dead of night the cry went up all hands splice the main brace, wouldn't you respond r The bishop was quite unprepared for the thrill which moved and then shook the audience. His dis- tress when I explained matters afterwards was very great.

"%IA you mind nawthen about that, sir, you couldn't have done it better," was the re- asauring comment of an old weather-beaten smacksman, who happened to meet the bishop the next day. The incident led to an interest- ing conversation between his lordship and my- self on the subject of sermons, and the danger of using technical terms. Afterwards at a Church Congress he made quite an interesting speech on the subject, but he did not quote Gorleston Parish Church.

SIDELIGHTS ON HISTORY. This recalls another Churchy incident. One day I was out on the North Sea fishing for whiting. My companion supplied me with information in regard to the most prominent landmarks. " That there church over there about west by south is Cotton old church it used to ba as big as the cathedral until Mr. Cromwell blew it up with gunpowder !" Then he gave me other information. " Mr. Cromwell's daughter kept the White Horse Inn in Gorles tou. This I believe was so. " Did you know Mr. Cromwell ?" I asked casually. "No, sir, you see it is some years ago now, but my father knew him well. They've 'ad many a think together in the Old White Horse,' so I've heard him Say, and 'weren't he dead on churches! But I don't think it were none o' his fault, sir, so I've heerd my father say. It was the Pope of Rome." An amusing incident took place during the last census. The official paper dealing with shipping population has a column in which the captain or other authorised person is req nested to write the names of all who slept on board the ship on the night of a certain date. This is how the skipper of a small schooner filled in his form. " There slept on board my ship last night three hims and one her." And then he added by way of further explanation. " P.S. They all slept on shore." " It won't do," I said, and entered into ex- planations why. " That's all very well for the likes o' you auiLme hut oou hiNve on idea bow stomaid them
unarm) chaps are. they woman 't ucherstar- unless I writ it like that." The mate ported him with sundry huts about the Cus- toms which would make an article in themselves so I dropped the subject.

div.head: WOMEN AND WESTMINSTER ABBEY.
div.p: WOMEN AND WESTMINSTER ABBEY.

A lady correspondent writes: "I was, some time since, visiting the Poets' Corner with a Frenchwoman. What?.' she exclaimed, as her eyes fell on the commemorative tablet to Jenny Lind; 'in an age which has produced Charlotte Brontë, Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Mrs. Gaskell, and George Eliot, is the only woman memorialised here a foreign opera-singer? How you Englishwomen can put up with such a slight on your sex passes my comprehension.' The French lady's astoundment is surely not to be wondered at. To say nothing of the four great women writers now familiar to every . reading people in the universe, others there asp who should certainly stand before a Swedish or any other foreign prima donna. There is, for in- stance, Barbara Leigh Smith (afterwards Bodi- chon), the foundress of Girton College and the bringer-about of the Married Woman's Property Act. There is Mrs. Booth, the mother of the Salvation Army, who brought solace and uplift- ing to hundreds of her outcast sisters. There is that heroic stewardess of the steamer that foundered a year or two back off the coast of Jersey, and who, after bundling women and children into the boats, with a calm 'Good-bye' —no room being left for herself—awaited her own doom on the sinking vessel. And these are not the only ones deserving of the highest honour their country can pay them." SIMPLE EVENING- FROCK.

The illustration shews a simple little evening frock of white teolienne. The low bodice is cut out in a square, and is outlined with lace inser- tion. The pretty corselet yoke is composed of white net, spotted with tiny gold spangles. It ts gathered very full, and outlined at the lower edge with another row of insertion; and then a narrow gold tinsel cord is crossed over the net between the two rows of lace. The belt, with

the long ends banging. down in front, is com- posed of white teolienne, lightly embroidered with gold thread, and fastened at the waist with a delicate gilt filigree buckle. The short puff sleeves are gathered into bands of in- sertion, and finished with two full frills of spangled net. The skirt is full, and quite plain except for a row of insertion above the hem.

div.p: PIRLE FINISH.

Is there anything more annoying to the woman whose dress allowance is by no means in- exhaustible than to discover that a new gown is spoilt the first time of wearing? asks a corre- spondent. It is one of the ills which assail us all during the months of November and Decem- ber, when rain and sleet and snow work havoc, and the moral of it is that we should make a point of securing material with a " pirle finish." A material treated in this way may be taken out on the most hopeless of wet days and will neither spot nor cockle up" as a result of the hardihood of its wearer. •

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

PARTRIDGES A LA RElNE.—Having plucked and cleansed three quite young partridges, split them in two and saute them with a chopped shallot in stewpan without allowing them to acquire colour; dust them with flour, add white stock to cover them, stir them together, and simmer the birds about an hour. adding a bouquet of parsley, onion, and a sprig of thyme. Mean- while, pare and scrape the gills from I.lb. of white mushrooms, chop them finely, adding a little lemon juice to -keep them white, then sstearn them with butter, salt, pepper, and lemon juice in a separate stewnan. Skim the sauce of the partridges, remove toe bouquet, stir in toe mush- rooms, add seasoning if necessary, and, at the moment of serving, stir in gill of cream pre- viously beaten -with the yolks of two eggs and a little milk,

div.head: HEA KT ON'
div.p: THE HEA KT ON'
-I:IIE SAILOR- MAN.

One grand trait in there men is their love of children. " How is the lir maid, sir ?" I had just been to see the little one, and this burly giant with a fist like a leg of mutton, and a voice like the rumbling of distant thunder, left a group of his companions to put a kindly ques- tion to me about a sick child—the parents of the child were strangers to him, but there was a world of sympathy in that enquiry about the "BB maid." The rough l'ikings have the big hearts of children—in a way they are children. The tears came to his eyes when I shook my head and said, " She is very ill." Some captious critic may Fay what has this to do with comedy in a fishing village. Only this. One aspect of their character would give an incomplete impression, and thererore a mis- taken one. These men are often represented as a God-forsaken, drunken crew, whose time ashore is spent in ribaldry and profanity. They are not teetotallers. They are not perfect. but their character, when all is said tor 80 against, remains grand. Braver men cannot be found. Their life is devoid of all that makes it tolerable to the majority of people. They take hairbreadth ercapes and face what looks like certain death as everyday matters of course that call for no comment further than " Ay, lad, Cwas a bit rough, but I'm 'ere, thank God.•' How often have I heard this. For these men have not lost their faith. Their language is sometimes strong, a bit of smuggling never loses its attraction, and a wreck is a rightful heritage, but their character can bear many ' minor defects of this kind and still be grand.
HEROISM AND SEAMANSHIP.
Two men I knew were washed off their ship. They managed to secure a broken fish-trunk sufficient to float one but not two.

'This ain't going to hold us both, Dick," says the younger man. " An' I would rather face the Almighty than your missus and tlw kids without you. Good luck." and he disap- peared from sight. A smack had to be abandoned in a sinking condition. There was teheavy sea running. The men had to take, their dinghy and begin the struggle for life under the most desperate con- ditions. Just as they had got nicely clear of the vessel—and those whose faces have been washed in salt water will know all that means —one of the hands cried out, " Why we have forgotten the kitten," there was no hesitation. The boat waktiwung round, they boarded the sinking smack gain. and brought away the little companion safely. England must remain mistress of the sea Co long as there are men like these to draw upon. The blood of the old 'Viking rovers throbs in their veins. They, as their forefathers before them, live by the ben ; as babes they are lulled to sleep, some on its bosom, all by its music. They understand its every whisper—read its humours and profit by its warnings. When -the broad ocean shudders and leans heavily against the laud, the true child of the sea knows what to expect and acts accordingly. This is sea- manship—the seamanship that has made Eng- land what she is to-day, and this seamanship means something more than a knowledge of navigation' and a certificate in steam.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Organ Recital.

The second of a series of monthly recitals by Mr. Ernest Wilkes was given in St. Paul's Church on Sunday evening, and was listened to by a large congregation. The numbers selected included "Fantasia pastorale " (Wely), which was admirably rendered. Master T. Barton played with skill the " Largo " (Handel), and during the service the choir sang Gounod's " The peace of God."

div.head: Bold-street Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bold-street Wesleyan Church.

Special services were held in the Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Sunday when the pulpit was occupied morning and evening by the l‘Rev. Professor J. Hope Moulton, M.A., D.Lit., of Didsbury College. At each of the services there was a good attendance. In the morning Professor Moulton based his remarks upon the contents of some old manuscripts found in Palestine four or five years ago, taking as the theme for his dis- course "Jesus, the way." The anthem "Nearer, my God, to Thee" was tastefully rendered by the choir. In the evening "The day Thou gayest "and by special request of the Rev. Moulton "Crossing the bar "was also rendered by the choir. Mrs. Arthur Booth sang "Lead, kindly light " in a praiseworthy manner, Mr. F. Hickman presiding at the organ. The rev, gentleman chose for his text in the evening" And Jesus entered into a ship and went over the sea to Capernaum. And it was now dark and Jesus was not come to them," preaching an eloquent sermon which was listened to with much attention. The collections were in aid of the society funds.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

The usual meetin,, was held on Sunday last when Mr. J. Owen presided. The speaker was Councillor T. Ogden of Urmston who spoke upon "Good possessions," which he said were within the reach of all who were obedient and faithful to the great giver of every good and perfect gift. Mr. Robins and Mr. D. Owen also took part in the meeting. Master Pearce presided at the organ.—On Monday night a fruit banquet, and concert took plane in the Memorial Hall Wycliffe, the attend- ance was rather disappointing, about 200 being present. Rev. John Yonge presided and regretted very much, the room was not packed as on previous years. Rev. .1. Davidson of Newton-le-Willows gave a sliort address. The following artists took part in the concert: Mr. J. Willett, "An evening song"; the Misses Jessie Farrar and Gladys Atherton, Pianoforte duet ; Mr. T. Brough's Juvenile Choir sang," The Veteran's song"; Mr. C. Furness recited three Lancashire pieces in his most amusing style; two children of the Juvenile Choir, Miss Dunn and Master T. Tanner, sang " Gipsy Countess," being encored they gave "Sweet Genevieve"; Mr. Pearce sang "The Bugler"; Miss A. Griffiths sang "Angus McDonald"; Miss Griffiths and Mr. Pearse joined in a duet, "The Spider and the Fly" Mr. A. Griffiths and Mr. Pearse duet, "Flow gently Deva"; Mr. W. Rutter gave a earnet solo "Queen of the earth"; the items in the programme were all splendidly executed. The Secretary voiced the thanks of the meeting to everyone who had helped to make the meeting so enjoyable. Fruit was served at 9 o'clock.
Madame Clara Batt and berhusband (Mr. Kennerley Rumford) who visit Warrington on December 13th, on Wednesday paid a visit to the Spring Grove Council, Huddersfield, and heard the scholars sing.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
NOVIMBER 25th 1906.
In some matters Mr MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S CLIAMBERLkIN is a FANFARE, good judge. He is

ssldorn mistaken in an election cry. The"crystallisation" about a vote against the Government being a vote given to the Boers was a contemptible piece of word-play, no doubt; but it did its work. The Chamberlain cry for the next General Election is, it appears, to be "More work for the people." it will be found no doubt, to have a considerable amount of effective- ness. There are many thousands of men of quite respectable education who really and sincerely believe that to keep foreign goods out of the country would be a good thing for ourselves. They think that what we do not bay from abroad we should make at home. This is the root of Mr. RICHARD SEDDON'S fallacy. The New Zealand Premier told us, with the bluff positiveness of full conviction, that we pay for our imports in minted gold. He did not pause in his haste to ask himself whether New Zealand pays for her imports in ia similar way, or he would, naturally, have been struck by the fact that she has not this means of paying, and that her imports are, in fact, paid for in mutt.n and wool. It is easy to understand that to people addicted to Pass such rapid and casual jedgments as those of Mr. SEDDON, it must seem a matter of certainty that if we import any manufactured article from Germany—it is Germany that is always taken in illustration nowadays—we must pay for it in money that should have been paid away in wages to our own industrial classes. We do not hold Mr. CHAMBERLAIN among those who hold this simple belief. He has a sound, if not a deep knowledge of political economy, and there is nobody living, not even Mr. Aseurre, who could reply more ably and convincingly to the economic heresies which he is now scatter- ing broadcast than he could himself. It suits him at present to set forth with an air of serious- ness, fire, and passion certain shallow theories which have been refuted in his former speeches, and of these the theory that Protection would pro- vide more work for the people is the worst, the shallowest, but by far the most attractive. It;,

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: therefore, becomes most necessary to insist that when the foreigner sends goods to 113 he is paid in goods of our own making. A single minute's consideration should be enough to make it appear that we do not, as Mr. SEDDON believes, pay in gold. We do not possess the gold necessary for the purpose. We do not dredge gold in our rivers, or dig it out of our mines. It does not grow. Gold is one of our imports. We pay for it, as we pay for everything else,in the goods we import from abroad, or by the services of our ships, or by our gains in commerce. When the foreigner sends commodities to us, he is really doing what Mr. CHAMBERLAIN merely promises to do—he is providing ,work for the people. A few simple figures will illustrate this point. If we are a great importing people we are also great exporters; the greatest in the world, in fact. France exports goods to the value of £3 153. per head of its population. Germany exports goods to the amount of £4 is. id. per head. And what is the value of the exports of Great Britain ? It is £0 17s. hi. per head. And this large export trade represents in the main work done by our people in exchange for the commodities we import Whatever be their character, whether they c3nsist of raw Or manufactured material. Mr. oNA:l=E- l...us's policy proposes to restria importation by means of tariffs. We are to keep out goods made in other countries and manufacture similar goods for ourselves. It is a pretty, irresponsible sort of doctrine, which, unhappily, will not bear thinking about. When we begin to shut out foreign goods by means of a Protectioinst dyke,we shall ,decrease tie work of the people to that extent,uot increase it. We shall have taken means to curtail our industries, and the first step towards that national ruin which is as certain to follow Mr. Orcuussit- Laix's policy as night is to follow day.

The agitation for the THE TAXATION OF taxation of land LAND VALUE. valn6s is making headway, and is now °tie of the most pressing domestic reforms which will claim the attention of the forthcoming 'Liberal Government. A conference of municipal

and other rating authorities from all parts of the country W5B held in Manchester on Taesday. A resolation was unanimously passed record:ng the urgent need tor legislation to provide for the assessment and rating of land values. A further resolution was carried urging the rating authori- ties of Great Britian and Ireland to support the new Bill which the conference will euhinit t Parliament. In the discussion reference was made to the rise in the value of land, and an opinion was 'erpressed that when unearned increments could be appropriated to the service of the community the settlement of the unemployed question and the housing question would be at hand.

Beautiful Warring- 'STOCKToN HEATH'S Nsw ton is—only tern- GARB. porarily we hope— being outstripped in the artistic race by Stockton Heath. The latter has youth on her side, and therefore possesses considerable advantages for personal adornment over her time-worn neighbour. New bricks and mortar, however, do not suffice, and the. tree- plaritre made a tremendous start in another direc- tion on Saturday. About forty young trees were planted by different inhabitants, and the wealth of twig and foliage is almost enough to persuade Young—very young—birds that it is springtime in the village. More trees are corning, we hear, and if a place is found for all in the confines of the is will soon bid fair to r.val the prirnev4l forest in the density of its verdure. If the Ship 'Canal Company does not object in the interests of navigation, the banks of the waterway for a mile or so will also be treated with a strong vegetarian—or should it be vegetationary— preparation, and sylvan scenery capable of charm- ing the eye of the hardy mariner will, in course of time, be ensured. Even the swing bridges are not secure from the invasion, though we hear that the soil here is rather thin,except on wet days. What Warrington will do, to remain in the running,it is difficult to say, but she might carry the war into the enemy's camp by roof-gardens on the trams. That she will "knuckle under" to her young sister is not to believed. Look at Arpley cannons! There is pride in the ancient bosom still.
NURSES' SUNDAY.

Twelve months ago we strongly advo- cated the inaug,nra- tion (IA a Nurses' Sunday on which colsections Would be made in all places of worship in War- rington or. behalf of the D strict Nursing Associa- ' tiou. We are pleased to note that there is the Possibility of an Emig realization of such a pro .ject for at the annual meeting of the Association on Tuesday, Mr. A. J. Jolley, whose services as secretary to the Hospital Sunday movement are highly appreciated, was requested to take this, additional work in hand and, if po4sible, to pre- vail upoi the representatives of tho churches to make an annual effort for such an extremely deserving cause. It is time Kll the religious bodies realized their duty in this matter for, in out view, the Nursing Association has an eqaal claim With the Infirmary upon their support. The need for funds was never more urgent, .. • kfor although the debt on the Nurses's Home has . •,'" :just been cleared off, a deficit of nearly 42,00 . ' I remains. There can he no two opinions its to the inestimable service which the "Queen's Nurses" willingly render to people who are unable to help ' 1 themselves, and their visits shed a ray of sunshine 1 into many a darkened home. Increased support is necessary and should be forthcJmiug —in fact wo • feel sure it will be if some organlzed method of ~ "enlisting it, like the proposed Nurses' Sunday, is li-successfully launched. ,

The scheme of co-. TiE GRAM:4AR SCHO3L. ordinating education in the borough will be advanced an important stage by the arrange- ment, approved at the meeting of the Education 'Committee on 31onday, under which the authority will eventually acquire a controlling influence in the management of the Boteler Grammar S.:hool. .Tnere is no Wore honoured scholastic institution in the district than this school which dates its foundation to 1526, and that it should take its Place as the highest rang in the local ecticcional ladder is but fitting. Toe scheme wh.ch has .just been agreed upon should make for the popularising—if one might be pardoned for using the term—of the school, as additional free si:tholan- 'shins will be awarded and the fees which have hitherto been prohibitive to many people will he educed. Important extensions of the building are in contemplation and when they are completed the school will be capable of accommodating, at least 150 boys, 20 per cent, of whom must be admitted by free scholarships. From a business standpoint, the arrangement appears to ha a sound one as the Corporation will be saved the heavy expenditrre of the erection and maintenano4 of a new school which the increasing demand for secondary education would probably have .entailed at no very distant date. All the authority Pledges itself to, financially, is the paymnt an annual deficit not exceeding £4OO. We trust that the school has, to use the words of •CanOn Morley Stevenson, " a great future before " and that its usefulness to all classes may be Increased as years go on.

Has Mr. Chamber- Tait UNIONIST PARTY. lain created a new Unwn at pavty or merely destroyed the old one? Whatever the answer—and we are inclined to apprehend the destrlctive rather than the constructive effect of the Bristol speech—the " Westminster G lntte has no doubt what type of party, whether new or ?Id, it is henceforth to be. "It is," says this Journal, " going to be a demagogue party and a

factious party. Its chief cry for the next election is to promise that unemployment will be cured by taxing the foreigner. Everyone is somehow to be made richer by making everything dearer. The Lonthm docker is to pay more for his bread, and, since imports are to .be diminished, he is to get less work at the docks. One would suppose from hearing Mr. Chamberlain speak that there was no peverty in America, and that the German work- man got better wages for less work and more regular employment than the British work- man. One would suppose also that there was no difference between a protective tax and a revenue tax except that the former was paid by the foreigner and could be used for building battleships at the expense of the foreigner. AU these childish and groundless delusions are no 7f to be solemnly adopted by the Conservative Party and made the basis of a pro- fusion of promises—promises of work to the unemployed, of wealth to the manufacturer, of unending trade supremacy to the Empire. The demagogue and the Jingo here join hands, and their joint policy is to be forwarded by making trouble in the new Parliament. It is surely time for the more sober sort of Unionist to consider whether this is really his idea of the future of the Uiliouist Party."

There will be quite " a revenue of populars " in Stockton Heath by and by. * * * The recent New York elections pro—e our American cousins to be far more advanced than ourselves. "One many two votes," seems to be the rule rather than the exception.—" Punch." * *

Rumours of resignation and diBs3lution fill the air, and Parliamentary crises abound. We may have a General Election this year—it is not likely—but it seems certain that the battle of the polls will be in fall swing in less than three months. * * * The ill-fated Hilda started on her last trip on St. Hilda's Day. Last Wednesday's saint was St. Nfalo hitnself,after whom the place is named ; and Thursday's was a St. Gregory, of whom the Hilda's captain was a namesake.—" Daily Chronicle."

* * The credit that enables a public authority to borrow at more favourable rates than a commercial company emld is impaired by being extravagantly used. Worse still is the discouragement ta enlightened and benevo- lent enterprise.—" Standard." * 5 * Many local Liberals will probably like to avail themselves of the opportunity of attending the big Liberal demonstration at Frodsham this (Saturday) evening. The Earl of Crewe will preside,and the chief speakers will be the Right Hon. R. B. Haldane, K.C., M.P., the Hon. Lyulph Stanley, and Sir John Brunner, Bart, M.P.

* * * Mr. Henry Vivian, the Liberal and Labour candidate for Birkenhead, was selected by the Cardiff Trades and Labour Council, one of the most representative Councils in the country, to defend Free Trade in a debate with the "tariff reformers " at Cardiff last (Thursday) evening. Those of our readers who heard Mr. Vivian speak at Warringtou will have full confid- ence in him as a champion of the cause.

* * A lady correspondent writes us from Trefriw on the Conway, enclosing a number of choice flowers sent as still growing in the open air there. She speaks highly of the mildue3s of the climate there at this time of the year, and adds "no fogs are ever seen or have every been remembered." Perhaps they have another name at Trefriw ! But the district is undoubtedly a charming one and well-sheltered. * * * The following cutting from the " Transvaal Critic" Johannesburg, sheds a lurid light on the" happiness and prosperity " of our South African Colony under the British and Cosmopolitan Jewish regim.6 : We have set up another world record. Seven suicides reported in one week, and two more at the week-end is surely a register of broken hearts, wrecked lives, and reckless despair that no other community of like size could (to its disparagement) imitate." * * * . .

Stockton Heath has a one-man committee—but even then one man has resigned it seems. Mr. J. Whitley, one of the oldest and most respected residents,told the ParoAtial Committee on. Thursday night that he had done more work on the Lighting Committee than the whole or them put together. He had met by himself, visited the village himself, and passed resolutions . himself. The committee were so conscious of Mr. Whitley's virtues and their own shortcoming that they forthwith asked him to re-consider his resignation.

* Cycling from Winwick to Warrington the other day (writs a Manchester Guardian " correspondent), we were startled bye suddea awful sound that rose from a doleful groan in rapid crescendo to a shriek of unen- durable pain. An old lady walking on the footpath stopped with clasped hands, exclaiming, "Eh poor creature ! Whatever are they doing ?" She seemed so much upset and shocked that we felt bound to dis- mount and explain to her that it was only the siren at the County Council Asylum. aud not, as she appeared to think, one of the inmates. * * * Speaking at Stirling on Thursday night, Sir Henry Campbell-13annerman made a significent and emphatic declaration of his policy as regarded the administra- tion of Ireland. "The only way to heal the evils of Ireland's difficulties and her administration and give prosperity to her people and make her a strength instead of a weakneSs was," he said "that the Irish people should have the management of their own affairs. So far from his opinion on this score failing, it had become stronger, and, what was more, he had more confidence in its realisation." Thera is no Balfourian ambiguity about this declaration, and it should give satisfaction to the Irish Liberals all over the country. *, Many are the little wiles practised by public speakers. At a recent local function a gentleman apologetically began his remarks by telling the audi- ence that he' had not intended to make a speech on that occasion but moved by the enthusiasm of the moment he begged lesve to trespass &a." His_ flights into the realms of poetic eloquence were quite , impressive until he came to a sadden pause, on tile an attempt to recover himself, but failed. "You will r excuse me gentlemen" he said as he produced a care- fully prepared MS. and having found the place at which the trend of his thoughts was broken, com- placently resumed his discourse. ** * t most wicked parody of a very famous onnet has been sent to us by a gentleman who, in spite of it all, gives us to understand that he admires Wordsworth. It is called :

BALFOUR. SOLILOQUISES. The country is not with us; late or soon, We must resign ; we have abused our powers ; Little they prize a single pledge of ours; We have given ourselves away—a doubtful boon! This sea of Unemployed 'neath the cold moon, When winter winds are howling at all hours ; The gathering fear of want that lurks and cowers ; For this, for everything we are out of tune, It moves us not. Great Joe! I'd rather be

A Pasha governing by modes outworn ; So might I, reigning thee perpetuallee, Avause myself, and not repent the morn ; Have sight of Clifford drowning in the sea, Or help old Kenyon silence Frederick Horne. "Daily News."

* * Afr. Plinston's unfortunate entry into and with- drawal from the electoral field prior to the municipal elections appears to have almost set the Trades CDIIII- - and the Labour Representation Committee at loggerheads. There was quite a lively debate at the Trades Council meeting en Tuesday—in fact it reminds u 5 of a Town Council meeting—and soine of the tnetn- bars were inclined to be cross with the L.R.C. See- ing that all concerned made a mistake or two, what- ever differences exist should be bucied with amicable rites for the good of the Labour cause. Mr. Plinston was present, and wound up the discussion with a humble plea of guilty, and a pat on the back for the Societies which rejected him. If Mr. Plinston will, in future, be content to sail under one 'lag he may ulti- inalely find a place and a prefix on that select body, the Town Council.

Cycling Club Dance. The members of the Warrington Cycling Club held their annnal dance in the Parr Hall on Thursday evening when the proceedings were of a highly enjoy- able character. About 80 couples were present and dancing to music supplied by Mr. W. P. Bayley's band (Liverpool)" was kept up from 8 o'clock until 2 an. Mr. C. Wells discharged the duties of M.C. and was assisted by Messrs. J. W. Bibby, 3. Banks, F. Field; house, J. bray, E. Pickavance. The catering was in the hands of the 'Warrington CafiS Company.

The annual dinner in connection with the Warring- ton and District Bowling League will be held at the Lion Hotel on December 7th. During the proceedings the cup given by Mr. A. H. Orosfield and the medals for the winners and runners-up in the league competi- tion, will be presented. The individual merit medal will also be handed to the winner, Mr. A. Shaw of the Bull's Head team, who secured a similar trophy in 1904.

A meeting of the Junior Liberal League will be held at Gregory's Cafe on Monday evening when a paper on" The relation betweeii labour and drink" (a digest of the Lees and Raper lecture delivered by Mr. John Burns, M.P.), will be given by the Secretary Mr. 11. Gray. The Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Bolton) will hold an " At Home " at the Town Hall on Thursday from 3.30 to 6 p.m. The annual dinner and smoking concert in connec- tion with the Warrington District of the Ancient Order of Foresters will be held at the Lion Hotel, on Saturday, December 2nd. The second annual ball in connection with the Warrington Corps of the St. John Ambulance Brigade will be held in the Parr Hall on Friday, December Ist. The music NN ill be supplied by Mr. A. Starkey's band. Farther particulars will be found in our advertising columns. Madame Clara Butt, Mr. Kennerley Rumford and concert party will visit Warrington on December 13th, when they will give a concert in the. Parr Hall. Tickets can be obtained at Messrs. R. H. Pearson, Ltd., Bold-street.
Christmas Presents, Splendid New Stook.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge et., Warrington.—Advt. Warrington Builder's' Affairs. _ .

At the—Warrington Bankruptcy Court, on Monday, before Mr. Ridgway, registrar, an application was made by Mr. A. Browne for a receiving order against Peter Rigby, builder, Church-street, Warring ton.— The application wasA granted. Newsagent's Suicide. Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest at Warrington on Monday on the body of Mr. Pownall (62), a newsagent who resided with his son-in-law at 36, Oxford-street, Warrington, and who committed suicide on Monday.— It appears that deceased was taken home in a cab on Saturday night and complained of severe injuries. He said he had been leading his horse in the fog when the animal stumbled and fell upon him. On Monday night he was found hanging by a rope attached to a bed post. The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst of unsound mind." PUBLIC BENEerr.—IINOER TICS CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS DI LANCISIIIRE.—Advt. " bandy Dick." - -•- -

The concluding performance by the members of the Warrington Dramatic Society, of ' Dandy Dick," was given in the Parr Hall on Saturday eveaing,. The audience was larger than any which had assembled earlier in the week, and the proceedings were highly successful. The excellent standard of acting was fully maintained, and the audience was not slow to show its appreciation of the merits of the parformance. .Each lady artiste has been presented with one or more bouquets and a box of chocolates, and some of the gentlemen have had presents chieffy of an amusing character. The thanks of the society am due to Mr. H. M. Ashton for so kindly booking the seats.

Bravery Recognized. Mr. W. Harding, an employe of Messrs. W. D. HouOton Ltd., will on Saturday night week, be the recipient of the Royal Humane Society's certificate on vellum in recognition of his bravery in saving a childs life. Harding was at work when a little lad who was playing on the banks of the Sankey and St. Helens canal, fell into the water. Harding jumped into the canal and with difficulty rescued the lad, almost los- ing his own life in the attempt. By his request the presentation of the certificate will be made by Prov. G. M. Bro. Joseph Taylor, at the lodge meAting of the Prince of Wales Lodge of Oddfellows (MX.) of which he is a member.

Large stack.—J. S. CLItLAND, 51 to 55; Bridp; st., Warringt am—Advt. • Drank Carbolic Acid. An inquest was held at Warrington on Tuesday on Jane Tomlinson, 3, Annie-street, Warrington, who died on Thursday from the effects of carbolic acid poisoning.—James Tomlinson said his wife was 32 years of age. She had for some months been in a very weak and depressed condition. —Sergeant Barlow said he was in the neighbourhood of Annie-street on Thursday afternoon when he was informed that Mrs, Tomlinson had taken poison. Dr. Peacock°, who was in the street at the time, examined the woman and pronounced life extinct.. Round her mouth and throat were signs of severe burning by corrosive fluid, and there was .1), strong smell of carbolic acid. On the table he found a battle which contained carbolic acid. In his opinion the woman died from carbolic paison- ing.The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst of unsound mind.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, KC., Messrs. Chinon's, Ltd., brought an action against Mr. Frederick I,)ingley, [lands worth 13irminghtinv to recover £ll 7s. 6d. money due from the defendant to the plaintiff.—:Mr. Browne appeared for the plaintiffs and said that out of 80 eases which Messrs. Garton's Ltd., had had hi Court that morning that was the only contested claim.— It appears that defendant, who was the Birmingham representative of the plaintiffs collected certain sums of money on behalf of his employers which he had not handed over.— Defendant admitted the debt but said he hal not paid the money as plaintiffs would not supply him with a statement as to the commission which he had corned. —Mr. Browne painted out that according to the agreement the state- ment could not be given to the defendant until Ie had handed over all money collected by him on behalf of the plaintiffs.As soon as the m )ney wa paid the statement w4dbe supplied to the de fendant.Rl a ntiff's agents were paid commission according to the amount of money which they collected.—Judgment was given far the plaintiffs with costs.
