Createlds' Band The quartette party from this band was again on Saturday last successful in winning a prize, this time the second prize at the Eccles Contest, The full result was : Ist, Atherton Public, 2nd, Crosfields, 3rd, Wingates Temperance, 4th Hanley. There were twelve competing sets. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASb MINERAL WATERS.—Advt. P.S.A. Meeting. There was a 1 trge attendance at the weekly meet- ing of the Warrington P.S.A. Society, which was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Sunday. Mr Smiley presided, and gave a short address on "Sowing and reaping," while Mr. W. W. Drewett spoke upon " Christ and the home." Mr. Cade sang a solo in a very effective manner. Mr. B. Wadsworth was the accompanist. Councillor Clegg and the President also tack part in the meeting. Harriers 'Warrington Wesleyans, bad as visitors last Saturday a strong team from Suttou. The pack numbering 32, turned out from the Unicorn at 3.15, 7 miles of hard country were traversed, by way of Bewsey and Burtonwood. After an absence of about 50 mins. C. J. Straw arrived, followed by a club mate, Bolton of the Wesleyans finishing 3rd. Result: Sutton Harriers, Straw, 1; Bradshaw, 2 • Morris, 4; Colquitt, 7; Colville, 8; total, 22. Wesleyans, Bolton, 3; Mellor, 5; Vose, 0; Worsley, 9: Jepson, 10; total. 33, PUBLIC BENEFIT. UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—AdVt. Not For the Army. At Warrington, on Wednesday, Joseph Nolan was charged with enlisting in the 4th Battalion The King's (Liverpool Regiment) on the 11th inst., under a false declaration. It was stated by an officer that on April 1 this year prisoner enlisted in the North Lancashire IRegiment, and was discharged for misconduct. He I afterwards went to Liverpool, and enlisted in the j King's Liverpool Regiment, making a false declara- tion. Prisoner, who had been previously convicted for a similar offence, and also for burglary, was sent to gaol for three months with hard labonr. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL WATER S.—Advt. Popular Penny Concert. There was a crowded attendance at the popular penny concert held in Bold-street Wesleyan Schools on Saturday evening. A highly interesting pregramme was submitted and every item was well received. Miss Eckersley very pleasingly sang "Bid me to love" and " Angus Macdonald '. and Miss Griffiths gave " Love the pedlar" with good effect. Mr. Pearce was heard to distinct advantage in " Revenge " and " The Admiral's broom," and Mr. Griffiths acquitted him- self very creditably in " Good company " and " Death of Nelson.' Duets by Miss Eckersley and Mr. Pearce, Miss 'Griffiths and Mr. Pearce and Messrs. Griffiths and Pearce formed enjoyable items. Mr. W. Rutter was warmly applauded for two cornet solos " When other lips ' and " The holy city." A conjuring entertainment by Mr. White quite mystified the audience. The concert was presided over by Councillor Brough who expressed his entire sympathy with the movement and said all praise was due to the Rev. J. Vanning for inaugurating it. LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIO GE-STREET.—Advt. Warrington Trades Council. The monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council was held in the Bold-street schools on Monday, Mr. Plumb presiding over a good attend- ance.—Councillor Stott said he had written to the Mayor, as instructed, asking him if it was possible for some of the Council Committee meetings to be held in the evening in order that the workingmen members might be able to be present. A reply had been received stating that the question was not for the Council but for the various committees. Mr. Plinston explained that a numbor of parents in Warrington had been circularized by a special com- mittee of the Education Committee,asking them if they were agreeable to their children being examined by the Medical Officer of Health, with a view to ascertain- ing if they were in any way medically or physically defective. The object of the committee was to place such children, if it was possible, in special schools for education. In Warrington, they could not at present afford to establish a) school as it would involve heavy expenditure. Medical examination would cost the parents nothing for such a purpose.—lt was announced that the Glass Makers' Union had decided to join the Council. A discussion ensued upon the representation of trade unionists on the Warrington Distress Com- mittee. Couucillor Stott explained that not having time to call a special meeting of the Council, he and Councillor Wright. had had the name of Mr. John Haley,'a prominent wire drawer, Placed on the Com- mittee.—lt was decided to endorse the action of the secretary. TINDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS.—Advt. Church Temperance Bazaar at Liverpool. Many Warrington people visited an attractive bazaar which was held in St. George's Hall, Liverpool, in aid of the Church of England Temperance Society on Tuesday, Wednesday mid Thursday. The large hall presented an animated and picturesque scene, and the decorations were such as to show to the greatest advantage the beauty of the 'goods on sale. The stalls were erections of latticework and Moorish screens in white wood, with tent-like drapery of pale green and , white. Very Pleasing was the arrangement of the platform with carved pillars and pedestals, surmounted by trellis work, and with banging draperies of delicate green. The flower stall had overflowed to the front of the platform, where tall chrysanthemums and clusters of variegated foliage adorned the steps, and made a charming border in front of the white rails. The effect of this daintily-decorated platform was particularly noticeable when it was occupied by the Tunisian Ladies' Orchestra. The objects of the bazaar are to remove the deficit for the last year, and to assist in providing funds for the continuance of general , temperance work, the Police Court and Prison Gate Mission, Women's Union and Terriperauce Home, Band of Hope lectures and the workrooms for men and boys. There were stalls arranged by supporters of the society ia varioae parts of the fAlvtri»ol di ces° The War- rington and District Stall was well supplied with , fancy articles and handsome embroidery, and was under the management of Mrs. John Fairelough, assisted by Mrs. Carleton, Ml's. Kelp!' Johns :n, Mrs' Peter Rylands, Mrs. Morley: Steveason, the Misses Tinsler, and Miss Alice Daunt: The bazaar was opened on Tuesday by the Hon. Rose Bootle-Wilbraltain Lord Derby presiding. Oa Wedricsday the ceremony was performed by Lady Reyden and ort Thursday by Mrs. William Gainble. H. M. ASHTON'S Ides ToNlc- takes away that ti red feeling.—( Advt.) ' Death of a Local Crimean Veteran . - _

The death took place on Wednesday, at his resi- dence, Inkerman Lodge, Greetby-hill, Ormskirk, of Sergeant-Major J. L Nunnerley, of the 17th Lancers (" Death or Glory Boys "), and one of the " Six Hundred." Deceased, who was in his seventy-fifth year, had a remarkable career, A native of Wilders- pool, near Warrington, he was apprenticed in 1814 to a draper in Warrington, but, having a strong desire for a soldier's life, he joined the Army two years later, enlisting in the 17th Lancers, and joining the regiment at Dundalk. He remained in Ireland with the regiment until the year 1851, and while stationed in Dublin in 1848 assisted in quelling the rebellion of Smith O'Brien, the then member for Limerick. In 1854 Mr. Nunnerley was ordered with his regiment to the Crimea,where he took part in the most famous battles, including Bulganack, Alma, M'Kenzie's Farm, the taking of Balaclava fort and harbour, be Balaclava charge, inkerman, Tchernaya River, and the whole of the siege and taking of Sebastopol. When the reduction of the Army took place in 1857, Sergeant- Major Nunnerley left the service owing to not having eceived the just and reasonable reward he had . merited during the eleven years he had served in the 17th Lancers and in the Crimean campaign. He . held the position of stationmaster at Dislev for two years, and then the late Earl of Lathom offered him the post (which he accepted) of . drill instructor to the D troop of the Lancashire Hussars, which his lordship formed. He acted in this capacity for twenty-two years, and on his retire- meat, through the influence of the late Lord Lathorn, his services in the 17th Lancers (from whom he took his discharge) and in the Yeomanry were recognised tiy a pension of Is. a day. Mr. Nunnerley was the recipient of numerous presents from the H4sars and . from the general public. His decorations included I. Ithe Crimean medal, the Turkish medal, and the I French war medal and diploma. On July 23, 190.1, . Sergeant-Major Nunnetley went to Garswood Park, near St. Helens, to receive a silver medal for meritorious " service conferred upon him by the King, together with ztifi annunity. Tins amount was subsequently increased to £lO per annuni. Sergeant-Major Nunnerley was predeceased by his wife a few months ago, and leaves no issue. He has a younger sister living at Stockton Heath.

Mr. John Blaginn's Sale. large numbers of townspeople have been attracted to the sale rooms of Mr. John Magian in Bridge-street and Rylands-street where an important sale by auction of household furniture commenced on November 15th, and will continue until December 2nd. The sale is an annual event but the goods displayed this year are stated to constitute the largest stock of household furniture ever offered for sale by auction in Lancashire being valued at over £6,700. Theie is a splendil variety of high class furniture and no fewer than 45 pianos and organs by well known makers are offered. Petroleum Oil in barrels and drums delivered free.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, bridge st., Warring- ton.—Advt. P.S.A. Social. The members of the Warrington P.S.A. Society held their first annual tes and social in the Co-opera- tive Hall, Sankey-street, cm Thursday evening. An excellent tea was provided to which about 70 sat I down, the tables being presided over by Mesdames W. Clegg and W. Jones and the Misses Oakley, Garnett and Clegg, assisted by members of the Society. The subsequent proceedings were of an enjoyable character and were presided over by Mr. Frank Hickman. Songs were given by Miss Evans, Mr. Hannan, Mrs. Hannan, Miss Lester, Mr. Pearce ; recitations by Mr. Wilcox, duets by the Misses Evans and Lester, Mr. and Mrs. Hannan, and Mrs. Hannan and Mr. Pearce. Mr. Scarisbrick was responsible for several excellent humorous sketches. St. John's Presbyterian Church.

I The members of the Christian Endeavour and the choir of the above Church had a very successful " Social "on Tuesday evening. There was a large attendance. The Rev. J. L. Milne presided. The programme arrangements were under the careful and skilful superintendence of Mr. Jowett, the organist. ' These consisted of a pianoforte solo by Miss M. Mills, a song entitled" Ora Pm Nobis " by Mrs. Ashton; " Rush me 0 Sorrow," by Miss Ditchfield ; " Marv," and the "The Last Milestone " by Mr. Forster; "The Larboard Watch," by Messrs. J. and E. Ditchfield ; gramophone selections provided by Mr. Win- stanley ; readings by Miss Dewar and Mr. Hemm- ings ; and a humourous dialogue entitled" Wanted a Wife," in which the Misses M. Brown, A. Brown, Dewar, Ditchfield, and Fraser, and Messrs. Ditch- field and Vose took part. Tea and fruit were served during the evening, the whole closing with games which all heartily enjoyed.

An open meeting was held in Friar's Gate House— the new quarters of the Society—on Thursday evening• Mrs. Dodds presided over a good audience. The meet- ing opened with a hymn and prayer: Mrs. Dodds, in her remarks from the chair, said she was very pleased to preside over so many young people, and that, at any time, she would be delighted to help the " Y " Branch in whatever way lay in her power. After a song f rom Miss Bridge, accompanied by Miss Crompton, Mrs. Dodds asked Rev. J. F. Matthews the speaker of the evening, to give his address. Mr. Matthews referred to the Temperance cause from several standpoints. He did not think from a political point of view that the Drink Problem would ever be solved till women were allowed a parliamentary vote. Then, too, he thought platform declamations were about" played out "as regards temperance. What was wanted was a better understanding of the evils caused by alcohol-1 fuller education. A step had been taken in this direction by a request signed by some thousands of the medical profession, that Temperance doctrines should be taught with Hygiene in the schools. Then he told his audience they most use their personal influence, they mustn't think they , hadn't any, because, if every man was a hero to some- ' body, so must every womin be a heroine to somebody else, and there were a lot of youog peiple, boys and girls, Just leaving school and going to work, who were in need of personal sympathy,their surroundings were not always of the best or purest.lt was to this class he earnestly exhorted the members to devote their time —a class which not many societies were able to touch but which they ought to find easier to do, as a mutull age and interests would create a bond.—Ms. Milne proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Dodds, M. Matthew*, and Miss Bridge, who had delighted the audience with her songs.—This was 83.1 laded by Miss Watson, and the meeting closed with the Doxology.

div.head: WATERWORKS UNDEgrAKING. --- Protests at a Local Government Board
div.p: THE WATERWORKS UNDEgrAKING. --- Protests at a Local Government Board
Inquiry.

Considerable interest centred in a Local Government Board inquiry held at the Town Hall to-day (Friday) by Colonel A. J. Hepper, D. 5.0., 1.E., into the applica- tion of the Corporation for sanction to borrow £l,OOO for waterworks purposes, viz., compounding of a beam engine at the Winwick pumping station. There was a large attendance of members of the Property Owners' Association, councillors • and ratepayers—Mr. A. T. Hallaway (deputy town clerk) =de the application on behalf of the Corporation and pointed out that the compounding of the engine would secure increased mechanical efficiency: there would be less risk of break- down and a smaller amount of wear and tear. Councillor PENrururroN, who complained of his diffi- culty in obtaining information, asked Air. Deis (water engineer) a series of (motions. Air. Deas denied that the engine would be used simply as a "stand-by." The engine had not been worked since July 1904. A break- down occurred and that led to the idea of compounding . it.

The IsseEcTort expressed surprise that so much interest was being taken in " so small a subject." Mr. H. J. Losurox contended that thealteration was not necessary as there was sufficient engine power. If the expense were incurred it ought to be,provided out of the revenue of the undertaking. Mr. JAMES Donns followed on similar lines.

The INSP&CTOR said he hardly saw the force of the argument, as in any event the ratepayers would have to pay. Mr. DODDS said the expenditure should be charged to revenue as an object lesson to the ratepayers who had had the loan debt rushed up a million • and a half during the last few years through laxity and extravagance by ru3mbers of the Town Coun- cil who were now in a minority, sppported by two or three officials whom they wanted to get rid of. Councillor PEMBERTON contended that all that was necessary Was that the engine should be repaired and not compounded. Alderman SMETEIURST and Councillor WitglssoN supported the application. Alderman BENYETT in reply to Aft. Dodds s tid he objected to being made a into martyr for the sake of an object lesson. Messrs. W. lIICKM.A.N, HENRY MORNTON, S. G)L7Gtf and others also opposed the application and the inquiry was then closed.

WESLEY G m.o.—The literary detachment bad charge of the meeting on Wednesday night, aud MUCiI amuse- ment was derived from the" maiden efforts " of the members as impromptu speakers. The President Rev, A. Cecil Parker presided and ha', drawn up a list of four subjects to speak upon. The speakers left the room, and were called in in rotation, and shown the list, and on picking a subject, were supposed to speak at once upon the matter. The speakers were inure or less succvs- ful, hut the task wits rather too much for the majority. The subjects submitted were : " Is war justifiable ? " " Should Christians take part in polities ?" " What do you consider the most admirable qualities, that go to make true womanhood and manhood ?" and" What do you consider the best methods, to induce young members to attend Chapel." The members taking part were, Mrs. Dodds, Miss M. Dodds, and Miss A. R. Boardman, j and Messrs. Murphy, Walker, Faulkner, U. Carman, El. Cirman. The voting of the audience deservedly awarded the palm to Mrs. Dodds, who spoke very fluently and pointedly. A further experiment on the same linos will no doubt be more successful as this is the first occasion the idea has been exploited.

EMMANUEL CHURCH. , ANNUAL SALE OF WORK OPENED BY MR. A. H. CROSFIELD. 1 The Church and Social Work.

e The workers of Emmanuel Church are engaged in an effort by means of their annual three days sale of work to raise £3OO which is needed for an exception- ally deserving object. A commodious building was recently acquired in Knutsford-road, known as Emmanuel Church Institute ", and it is hoped to make use of it for various admirable purposes. Many schemes,it is stated in an appeal which has been issued, ' are being devised the future, including free club ! room for men,social work among women and children, temperance, mission, and other institutional work which only await the necessary funds to carry to a successful , issue. Situated as it is, in a densely- populated neighbourhood, the Institute will lend itself readily to this work. The project is unfortunately hindered by the burden of a heavy debt on the premises, in addition to the strain of raising annually, minister's stipend, ground rent, repairs, current expenses, and the many minor difficulties which con- stantly present themselves to a poor, though large- hearted congregation. MOO is asked for to enable the workers to meet existing liabilities and carry out some of their plans for the future. I The sale was opened in the Chumh Institute on Wednesday afternoon and will continue until this (Friday) evening. The ladies have entered into the ! project with considerable enthusiasm and the stalls, which are most attractively arranged, contain a great assortment of saleable wares. The following are the names of the stall-holders : Minister's stall : Mesdatues F. Vaughan, Liudle, A. Dickens, and R. Lees. Congregational stall: Mesdames : G. Norman, W. Armstrong au d D. Wright, Miss Landon, and Mr. E. Allen. Sunday school stall : Mrs. A. Gandy, Mrs. W. Atherton, Miss A. Minards and Mrs. C. Lloyd. Children's stall : Misses A. Booth, E. fournival,, M. [both, L. Vaughan and N. Vaughan. , Refreshment stall : Mr. T. Allen, Mrs. A. Landon, Misses B. Lees and C. Jenks. Flower and, fruit stall : , Mr. and Mrs. J. Callan, Misses Heald and D. Shepherd, and Mr. W. Minards. Tea room : Nferlarnes B. Allen and Shepherd, Misses Annie Ali:lards, J. Allen, and Millicent Allen.
OPENING BY MR. A. H. CROSFIELD. THE CEIERCEIES AND SOCIAL WORK.

The sale was opened on Wednesday afternoon by )Ir. A. IL Croslield. The proeeclings were presided over ,[ by the Rev. John Yonge and amongst those present were :—The Rev. Frank Vaughan (incumbent), Alder- man Tinnion, Messrs. J. Critchley, E. Lecker and W. ' ' Biebv. - [ The CLEATIOLIN baid it had been his pleasure and [ privilege to be present at the majority of the sales of 1 [ work held in connection with Emmanuel Church of recent [ I years and he had always taken a great interest in them. They always appeared to him to be one of the signs of . [ life connected with the Emmanuel people in which they I were endeavouring to help thezuselves ia a very laud- , able manner. In days gone by they had scored some very distinct successes at their sales of work and ,he hoped that [would be so on the present occasion. , [ Ile believed that building was raisin a great many ' [ memories in the minds of some of the friends who were [ present, for they knew it in the days of yore when they • were scholars there under the original condition of ! things before Emmanuel Church was ever dreamed or [ thought of. It appeared to him a sort of poetic justice [ that the building should come back into their hands, and he hoped they welsh' in the years to come continue to make the good use of it which they had drawn up in their programme of work. It was pleasing to know . that their Church was entirely free from debt, but it had no endowment, neither did it obtain its income for current expenses from the old- fashioned source of pow rents. All the money , they received came from the free-will offerings of the ' congregation. He was certainly of opinion that that the soundest principle for finance in connection with church work. The new Church Institute had added to them the burden of debt—a very considerable one amounting to £1,400 which represented the purchase price of the premises and the cost of sundry structural alterations and fittings. They had to pay at present interest on the money which had been mortgaged to the tune of about £42 a year. lie heartily hoped that that was sale would raise the stun: they desired—£3oo—for [ seeing that their needs were so much greater their receipts ought to be larger than, was usually the case. With regard to the work of the Church Institute, there was plenty of virgin soil around them on every hand, and he hoped they would be able to give justification for their existence by draw- ing into the school and into their work generally a con- siderable number of the population of the district. The chairman concluded by expressing the pleasare all felt at the presence of Mr. A. H. Crosaeld who belonged to a family which'was deservedly held iLI very high and wide respect and esteem by people of all parties and of all churches in Warrington. (Applause). They were sure Mr. Croslield had every sympathy with the object of the sale and they were delighted that he had come to open it. (Applause). Mr. A. H. C110..i FIELD, who had a very cordial reception, thanked the gathering very sincerely and heartily for the kindness of the welcome they had given him. He also thanked Mr. Tongs for the kind things he had said about his (Mr. Crosfleld's) Mr. Yonge was quite right in saying that he (the speaker) felt the sincerest sympathy with the work that would be carried on in that building, and although he bed not had the pleasure of a close acquaintance with Mr. Vaughan he knew very well the really splendid, work he was doing in that part of Warrington- ( Applause). It was partly because he knew what assist- ance that building would be to Mr. Vaughan in carry ing out the varied programme he had undertaked that he so sincerely hoped that the bazaar would be the greatest possible success. Another reason that, of course, appealed to hint was the feet that they at Emmanuel Church as a religious body were self-supporting. Re believed,if he might say so, in the principle of self-help in connection with religious organizations as in other branches of life. He hail in the course of his life had the privilege of standing on a great Many religious platforms with men who in their creeds diverged widely and he had said before—and with all respect he ventured to submit it to them now—that the reason men like himself, engaged in oresamerce and politics, might come amongst friends who devoted themselves to religious work on an occasion of that kind was that whatever the difference of the religious creeds amongst them might be, there was the fundamental fact that men of the world like men of religion might grasp that what Matthew Arnold called " the untaowa power that makes for righteousness" was at the bottom of the whole of the religious endeavour of the country. (Applause.) He felt very strongly that that might bring them together and might also teach everyone of them a great lesson in the broad principles of toleration in which his late father brought him up. If it were not so, seeing bins on those different platforms they usieet think he was almost like another Vicar of Bray —(laugh- ter)—changing his beliefs with changing circumstances. It was nothing of the kind. That fundamental principle made all the difference in the world. And a third reason that influenced him very much and made him anxious to see that institution and other institu- tions of the same kind prosper in Warrington was the fact that the churches, if they were to exert their highest indaenoes and be of the greatest benefit to the whole of humanity, should not—if he might say so with all respect in the presence of the chairman—be content merely with the preaching of ' dogma but they should help to raise the civil life of the people amongst whom their lot was cast. That was precisely what the object of that Church Institute was going to be.lde didlnot think at this time of the day it was for any religions denomination to shut itself apart and say "We will take no cognisance of the affairs of the world, be they the affairs of our own country or the things that are transacted in foreign lands." They could not shut oil religion from the daily life of the people by a sort of water-tight corupartment, and if they coeld it would be a very had thing indeed. They could take cognisance, whatever their faith might be,of things that were going on around them and he was sure the ministers of religion mast feel as deeply an anyone'such a sad and tragic problem as they had before them in this country in thecoudition of the unemployed. Carlyle said that he knew nothing that was more tragic than the condition of the man who was honest and willing to work and could not find work to do. Fortunately for the honour of our country,' he hoped a question like that could he treated as anon- party question just as our beloved King was able to enter into the question of the housing of the poor without taking what in any way could be Called 3 party attitude on the question. In the same way, when one read of the frightful things that were going on, happily not in our own i beloved country but n so many parts of the world, ho felt that the churches might make their influence felt in the cause of true progress and humanity and he hoped they would do so perhaps a little more than had been done up to the present time. lit. Crosfield con- cluded by declaring the bazaar open and wished it the greatest possible success. (Applause). The Rev. F. Vauolf AN proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Crostield and the Chairman. He was sure the interest and sympathy of all present was with the words of Mr. Crosfleld and the ideals he had expressed. They had never before had Air. Crosfield or any other member of that family to open their sales of work and they regarded his presence e*, marking an epoch in the history of the Church. He (the speaker) believed that so long as their church was true to its fundamentals and to the principles which called it into existence, so long would it continue to receive the support an I the assistance of the public of lVarrington. (Applause.) Alderman Trs:groN: seconded, and the vote was heartily accorded. In.resmnding, the CITIIRMAN announced that the Young Women's Bible class had contributed £3 13s. Gd. to the funds as the result of their special efforts, and another donation of £3 had come to hand.

div.head: THURSDAY'S PIZOCEEDINGS.
div.p: THURSDAY'S PIZOCEEDINGS.

The sale was re-opened on Thursday by Mr. T. Wilson, of Liscard, the chair being occupied by Mr. W. Mason, of New Brighton. The Rev. F. VAUGHAN said that the donations sent to the sale of work fund were never so small as this year, the total amount, including £5 13s. 6d. raised by the young ladies' class, being £9 ss. The takings at the stalls made that sum op to £6l 12s. 7d. (4plause.) ENTERTAINMENTS.

An admirable series of entertainments had been arranzed and was much appreciated. Selections on the pianoforte and other items have been given in the sale room by Miss Ellen Gandy and friends. On Wednesday evening Master Toni Barton's juvenile orchestra and other artistes gave an enjoyable concert, and on Thurs- day evening the programme was provided by the Misses Cu!slimy, of Liverpool. The proceeds for the two days amonnted to £lO5.

div.head: WARRINGTON SENSATION.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON SENSATION.
SISTERS CHARGED WITH MURDER.

At. the Warrington police court on Tnesday, Beatrice Waterworth, single woman, (31), and Alicia Drury, widow, (35), both residing at 10, Russell-street, were charged with the wilful murder of the infant child of Beatrice IVa.terworth, some time in October 1001. It will be rememoored that the prisoners were before the magistrates last week on a charge of concealing the birth of the child. Brialy recapitulated the facts then stated were that in September of this year ‘Vaterworth gave birth to a child. The day following her confine- ment Mrs. Drury's husband committed suicide, in con- sequence it was stated at the inquest which was held, of certain allegations made against him by the neighbours. The suspicions of the police were aroused Sy the receipt by the Chief Constable, and the Coroner of anonymous letters' andou the 15th inst they visited 63,Gmf ton-street, formerly occupied by the prisoners and Mr. Drury, and there after a brief search found the skeleton of a child buried in quick lime, under the pantry floor. At the proceedings on Tuesday Mr, Hallaway, deputy town clerk, who appeared to proseoute said very exten- sive inquiries had been made into the circumstances of the case, and certain new facts had come to light. In support of a charge of murder there ought to be the strongest possible evidence, anti he regretted, that they had not got the strongest possible evidence, as the women stood in peril of their liberty—even their lives —on ratherslight evidenee.But there WAS that, evidence,. though slight to consider. Another step had to be taken, as it was necessary that the circumstances should be reported to the Director of Public Prosecutions, ia order that he might th,troughly investigate them. He, therefore, asked for a remand until next Tuesday. Mr. Steel, who appeared on behalf of the prisoners, said he bad no objection to tho provided the Bench could See their Way to grant these miserable women bail. They had been in custody for over a week, and seeing that it WAS admitted that the evidence was very weak, he thought they might be granted hail. The Deputy Town Clerk said he wOuld not object to bail. • The Bench remanded the prisoners until Tuesday morning, bail being granted on their own security of £2O, and two other securities of .220. THE' INQUEST. SENSATIONAL ALLEGATION:3 BY Tar!. DECEASED MAN'S MOTEIER. AN OPEN V'ERDICT. The adjourned inquest on the remains of the child was held by Mr. S. Brighouse at the Police Station on Tues- day afternoon. Mr. A. T. Holloway (deputy town clerk) watched the case on behalf of the police, and the Chief Constable was also present.—Mr. Steel represented the prisoners. Addressing the jury the Coroner said the question they had first to decide was whether the chili had had la life to take away. The law assumed th at every per- son was born dead mull the contrary was proved and therefore when they wanted to charge any person with retarder or manslaughter they must first he satisfied that the child had a separate existence apart from the mother.

Dr. Reainald Smith, polies surgeon, said tke bones were those of a child of suliciant development that it might have been born alive. He was, however, quite unable to say whether the child had eseparate existence or even whether the recut:as were those of a male or female child.

Mrs. Eliza Drury, wife of John Drury, fish dealer, 69, Lairs-street, and mother-in-law of the prisoner, Alicia Drury, add th it it was her son ti,3on whom the inquest was held at Sankey in September. About six months h.fore the death of herson, her dtughter-in- law visited her house. In the course of the conversation prisoner said " I have committed murder for them and it is what they will not do far me." Further questioned witness said prisoner also said " Beatrice has been con- fined. it happened on a Siturday afternoon " and she added that she (prison3r) took the child into another room and killed It.
The Corouer : Are those the eat words she made use of? Witness : I are not quite sure whether she said she strangled it, but she led me to understand she had killed it.

-The Coroner slid it wis nat a question of what wit- ness understood but of the exact words used by Alicia Drury. Did she actually say " I killed it, " ? Witness : Shs did take its life b3O3,USE, she said " It did moan." Farther questioned by the Coroner witness could not give the exact words used by her daughter-in-law, and the Coroner remarked that they could not convict oa evidence like that.

Witness admitted that she told the Chief Constable that she had not been the satne in mind since her son's suicide. She had brooded over it night and day, had been very depressed, and still was depressed. , in reply to Jr. Steel (solicitor for the prisoners)the witness said she knew the child had been buried in the pantry five months before her son committed suicide, but she had not mentioned it to anyone because she thought her son might be imprisoned. When she hoard that detectives were about she becsme afraid. After ' the prisoner Drury mile the statement to her she gave her son a good talking to. The Coroaer rem trked that human life was too precious to be bartered away on such evidence. The jury thee retired, and' after an absence of a few minutes, the foreman (gr. E. Pickavance) amid they had cdrne to the unanimous conclusion that there was not the slightest evidence for them to decide whether the child was born alive or not, an!. they returned an open j verdict,
The Clraner intimlted that he agrood with the jury's verdict, end would hare acted in a similar in inner, had the nutter been in his own hinds.

The most important business under consideration at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Com- mittee on Monday evening was a scheme affecting the future of the Grammar School, which was presented for confirmation by the School Management Committee. Alderman Bennett presided, and there were also present : —The Mayor (Alderman Bolton), the Revs Canon Morley Stevenson, E. J. Willcocks. Father NVilson, and John Yonge, Councillors Btrton, Fulton-Smith, Lord, Sinkey, Wright, Evans, Ellison, Wilkinson, and Brongh, Messr.. A. J. Jolley, C. H. Unsworth, H. Kingdon, C. E. Parker, R. T. Feirclough, T. May, H. Roberts, E. Plinston, W. Bibby, G. Walker, and J. Moore Murray (Director of Education).
FINANCE CONINIITTEE. VIOLIN CLASSES AT DAY SCHOOLS.

At a meeting or the Finance Committee a letter from the managers of the St. Barnabas' School—suggesting the return of fees to certain children attending that school to meet the excess amount received during the past school year—was submitted, but it was decided to take no action in the matter. It was resolved that an intimation be given to the managers of the Heattiside National,Warrington British and Wycliffe British schools that the committee will make no charge upon the managers of those schools in respect of lighting, heating, and cleaning of the rooms which will be used for the purposes of the violin classes to be hold at those schools, until the 31st December, 1903, but that, after that date, the usual charge will be made if the classes are continued ; and that notice be given to the managers of the schools at which violin classes are already held, that, if the classes are con- tinued after the 31st December, 1903, the usual charge upon the managers in respect of the lighting, heating, and cleaning of the rooms %filch will be used for those •classes will then be made.
The minutes ware confirmed on the proposition of Mt. A. J. JOLLEY seconded by :klr. R. T. FAIRCLOCIOR. PEIVSICAL INSTKUCTION.

At a meeting of the Sch Management Committee the report of the sub-committee as to the arrangement made for carrying out the agreelient with the Gym- nasium Committee for tho instruction of school child- ren and others in physical exercises, was snbmitted and approved. The committee then had au interview with the two instructors employed by the committee, and outlined to them their wishes with regard to this matter. It was resolved, that all teachers of 28 years of age or under, who are engaged in schools maintained by this committee and who have no qualification for the teaching of physical exercises, be required to attend a class in that subject to be held at the Gymnasium from 6.30 to 7.30 o'clock each Weinosday evening ; and that arrangements be made for the teachers to be examined at the end of the course of instruction by the Examining Board of the British College of Physical Education,with a view to their obtaining a diploma of that college. Tn moving the adoption of the minutes Canon Nlorir.r:v STEVENSON expressed satisfaction that the negotiations n the subject had been happily terminated and that the committeee had come to an agreement and drawn up a working scheme which was already establishedand being carried out and which, he hoped, would work satis- factorily. THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL. • SCHEME EXPLAINED AND APPROVED.

The School Nlanagement Committee considered the proposals made by the Governors of the Warrington Grammar school at the recent Conference for the amendment of the draft scheme for the government of that school so that the representation of the Local Authorities upon the governing body might be propor- tionate to the amount of their financial aid, and it was resolved, that, in the event of the annual expenditure for the maintenance of the Warrington Grammar school exceeding the income, this Committee will make a grant to the Governors to cover the amount of the deficit, provided such grant does not, in any year, exceed the sum of £4OO, and that the Governors will continue to maintain the existing sixteen free scholarships and grant

Canon MORLEY STFIVENSON pee an interesting ex- planation of the scheme in moving the adoption of the minutes. He said that in 1526 the Grammar school was founded and given to Warrington. It was not. founded, as many of the grammar schools were, out of the proceeds of the revenues of disendovved monasteries or similar sources, but it was a free gift of a Warrington gentleman Sir Thomas Boteler. fie (the speaker) thought they would all feel proud of the fact that they owed the existence of the school with its handsome endowment to the gift of a citizen of this borough going back all that great lapse of time. It reminded them of the antiquity of the town, of the public spirit of the citizens, and of the generosity of which they had many noble instances in the borough, and it set before them an example which they would do well to follow. He did not intend to pursue the history of the school over that lengthened period. It would be obviously inadvisable to do so a!,thanks more especi; , ally to the efforts of the chairman, those who would could read it in the interesting pages of that magazine which shed so much light upon the antiqui- ties and the future of the town. Suffice it to say that coming down to quite modern times, there seemed to have been a somewhat p tinful lapse in the utility of the old school about the middle of the last century, and in the year 1860 the old build- ings which were, of course,quite inadequate for modern requirements were demolished. In 18113 so much of the present buildings as were comprised in the big school, a class room, and the headmaster's house, were erected. At th it date Mr. Carey entered upon his duties as head- master, and the school started into new and vigorous life. He had no doubt that many inhabitants of War- ringtoa at the present time could testify to the advan- tages which they had received during that period. In 1840 the school was still further brought up to modern requirements by a new scheme, and in 1831 Mr. Willcocks, the present headmaeter whom they were glad to see as a member of the committee, entered upon his regime. Since that time and under the influence and energetic supervision of the headmaster, the school had been immensely improved. Through the courtesy of Mr. Willcocks he was enabled to visit it the other day and to givea somewhat minute inspection to all the arrangements. Three good new class rooms had been added, a chemical laboratory and a physics laboratory, and it was now in contemplation, owing to the headmaster having removed from his house which was now able to be thrown into the building, to make a good room for manual work and two classrooms, one of which would take the place of the ole class-room which was somewhat out of date. In addition, excel- lent lavatory and cloak-roam accommodation was being provided and the entrance ball was being considerably enlarged and made lighter. When all that had been finished—and it would be completed before very long— they would have in the possession, so to speak, of the town a banding which was thoroughly well equipped and of which the arrangements were thoroughly efficient and up to date. Canon Stevenson alluded to the excel- lent results which had been obtained by the school. He did not think it was common that in a school of the size of Warrington they should meet with the number of University first rate distinctions of which the Grammar School could boast. There could not he two questious as to the efficiency of the instruction which had been given. The new scheme still further brought the arrangements of the school into harmony with the modern needs of the educational world. The school had now been recognized as a Secondary school by the Government and in every respect—its buildings, equip- ment, staff, management and teaching—he thought, they might feel confident that it had a great future before it. (Hear, hear.) There were certain points about which the committee had felt some anxiety. They desiderated a larger number of representatives on the managing body of the School than they used to hate under the old scheme and they were glad to see that the new scheme provided forseven representative managers

Mr. H.ROBEILTS said that while it was quite true that the negotiations were not terminated, the principles which were embodied in the proposals before the com- mittee that night, were agreed upon between the parties,and all that remained to be done was to arrange certain small details in regard to some of which he thought the School Management Committee would make one representation to the Board of Education and possibly the governors of the school would make another.

Councillor EVANS did not see why the con mittee should be asked to sanction the scheme before it was complete. The CHAIRMAN : It is really going to the Board of Education in this form. I think we shall leave the Board to arbitrate between us on minor matters.

IMr. ROBERTS said the governors had. irranticipation of something of this kind, and inconsequence of repre- sentations made to them by the Board of Education, got the school recognized as a secondary school, and in con- sequence had been compelled to incur a serious amount of capital expenditure, and increase the annual expendi- ture on maintenance in regard to the engagement of additional masters, &c. To meet that expenditure the only source of income open to them at the moment, exclusive of what the Education Committee might recommend, was the amount of grant earned on the specific subjects which came under the control of the Board of Education in consequence of the recognition of the school as a secondary school. It was not desir- able to anticipate that the deficitof a fairly largeamount should be allowed to be carried forward into a second or third year when it was the duty of the committee to come to the assistance of the school at the present time. So far as the supply of education in Warrington was concerned, the time had come when the Board of Education would have insisted that further accommodation for secondary accommodation should be provided and, assuming for the moment that the town, was not possessed of an endowed school of that character, it would be the duty of the committee to make representations to the Corporation to make that additional provision. A school of that kind, judging by the expenditure on the present secondary school, ' would cost very little short of £20,000. In addition to that the whole of the maintenance in connection with the administration of the school, less the fees received, would have to be found from the rates. Happily, however, they had in the Grammar School an institution which, speaking in the comparative sense, was so far as buildings were concerned very well equipped for the purposes for which it was intended. The Corporation would be saved the whole of the capital expenditure in connection with the land and buildings and the school had an income of between £BOO and £9OO a year which went to its up-keep. The scheme practically amounted to the Education Com- mittee taking over the school, because wnile it was pro- vided that for live years the management should be in essence what it at present was, at the end of that period the management would go by majority practically into the hands of the Corporation and two other public bodies. It was well known what his political and religious opinions were, and he could say with absolute certainty that the school provided would continue to provide, without any prejudice to the religions ' opinions or training of any of its pupils, the means for an education in the direction of professional life which would have to be provided by the Corporation if the school did not exist. As a business proposition it was a very good bargain for the people of this town. It was obvious, of course, that £4OO a year would have to come from the local authority, but the solace they might apply to their minds was : " hit better to pay £4OO a year or say £2,000 a year ?" The proposal, he believed, would confer advantages on the youth of the town for many years. In the course of further discussion the Director stated that £6 was the proposed minimum fee, but it did not , follow that all children would be admitted for that , sum.
Councillor WlLxixsoN said that he thought the inten- tion was to provide a large secondary school to accom- modate five or six hundred scholars.

div.head: Nurse Stone Speaks
div.p: Nurse Stone Speaks
Indigestion Cured, Strength Brought Back—A Message of Praise for Iron-Ox Tablets

div.head: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
THE FUTURE OF THE GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
Important Scheme Approved.

additional scholarships to be awarded upon conditions to be arranged between this Committee and the Governors so that the number of free scholars each year reaches 20 per cent of the total number of pupils in the school. It was also resolved, that the report of the Sub-Committee upon the draft amending scheme, approved by the School Nlanagement Committee at their meeting on the 21st September, and the report of the Conference held on the 12th October, 1905, with a deputation from the Governors of the Warrington Grammar school, together with the draft amending scheme as altered by the School Nfannagement Com- mittee, be submitted to the Education Committee for their approval ; and that the draft scheme as amended and approved by the committee be adopted and be submitted to the Board of Education.

out of a total of fifteen, thus raising the number from four to seven. Further, by special provision in Clause 5, additional governors might be appointed by the local authorities if they should give larger money grants at any future time. There was therefore a very consider- able increase in the amount of representation granted to local authorities under the new scheme, com- pared with that under the old. ft was true, of course as was always the case in these matters, that the existing managers would, so to speak, have to serve their time of five years, and the committee would all feel that it would be an extremely invidious distinction to ask any of them to retire in order to make the numbers fit exactly. Should any vacancy occur by death or any other cause, it would not be filled up until the numbers were brought down to the extent mentioned in the scheme. He honestly confessed that he did not consider the question of representation a 'matter or great importance. What he did think was important was that they should get men not so much as representatives of this or that, but men who were the very best educationists they could find. He was sure ' from their knowledge of the present governors of the , school, the Committee would feel they were not people that they would wish to part with in ' any way whatever. Another point which they felt to be of great importance was the fee to be charged. At present parents had to pay an entrance fee for their children of £2 and a minimum fee, in addition, of £B. The entrance fee would now be abolished and the minimum fee reduced from £8 to £6. He thought that would place the school within the reach of a larger number of people than had been the case in the past and he hoped they would soon see, when the scheme came into operation, a speedy increase in the number of 1 scholars. The committee were asked to sanction a grant to the school not exceeding £4oo—to put it plainly, they were asked to pay the deficit on the annual balance sheet, if there be one, and to safeguard themselves by saying that in no case would that grant exceed £4OO. lie thought when they considered what had been done by this benefaction in the past and the large sums that had been spent by the governors of the school in recent years in all the improvements he had endeavoured to describe, the town of Warrington would feel that it was entering upon a goodly heritage and it would be proud to do the very small part which it was asked to do in helping to maintain the school in efficiency. He did not think they should anticipate any serious opposition to the resolution, but lie thought it would be a gracious act if they could unanimously Agree to let it go forth to the town that the} were only too glad, as far as in them lay, to give that comparatively small measure of help for which they were asked. The Rev. Father WILSON seconded the adoption of the minutes.

Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGII thought the public ought to know how many scholars the new buildings would be capable of accommodating. The Rev. E. J. WILCOCKS said there were 98 pupils in the school this term. When the extension was com- pleted they would be able to take at least 150. Mr.INIA.v asked how the decrease in the amount of fees payable would effect the rates. He would like to know whether in return for the increased burden on the rates which the scheme) would entail, the committee would see that the benefits to be derived by all classes would be correspondingly increased or whether it was a benefit which was being taken from the poor and given to the rich in order to reduce the fees of those who were well ' able to bear the burden of educating their children. Mr. KING DON asked whether the committee was in order in discussing the scheme as he understood the negotiations were not yet completed. The CHAIRMA.N said that possibly it would be as well not to discuss the question at any great length as the negotiations were not absolutely settled, but the dis- cussion was quite in order as the scheme was on the minutes.

At a meeting of the School Management Committee a letter was submitted from the Chairman of the Edu- cation Committee (Alderman Arthur Bennett) offering for competition a shield in commemoration of the 100th anniversary of Trafalgar, and an annual prize of £l Ls. for the best essay on " National duty " or some similar subject ; the shield to be held each year by the school at which the successful scholar attends. It was unanimously resolved that the offer of Alderman Bennett be gratefully accepted; and that the Director be requested to prepare and submit to the committee at their next meeting a draft scheme for carrying out the competition. ' Canon STEVENSON said be was sure he would be expressing the feeling of the committee when he said , that they were most grateful to the chairman for encouraging the spirit of patriotism in the way he had so generously chosen to do. (Hear, hear.)

It is estimated that £1,000,000 worth of motor cars will have been bought by the end of the week at the motor show now being held in London. It is stated that the Great Central Railway Com- pany, instead of burying their rolling stock and material in the open market, are about to erect their own manufactories on a site already selected near Manchester.

LEARNT TO SWIM. Canon STEVENSON commented upon the return sub- mitted to the School Management Committee with reference to the attendance of boys from the public elementary schools in the borough at the baths. It was noted that, in all, 883 boys had attended the baths this season each on about ten occasions, and that as a 'result 79 boys had learnt to swim, 122 being already able to do so. If they could add a like or a greater number year by year, he said, the committee would do a great deal to promote an exercise which was as healthful as , it was useful. PUPIL TEACHERS' QUALIFYING EXAMINATION. The School Management Committee considered the question as to the qualifying examination for pupil teacbership to be taken next year by the scholars I attending the preparatory pupil teachers' classes, and it I was resolved ; (a) That application be made to the Board of Education for permission to hold a local , examination under Article 2 (c) of the regulations for the instruction and training of pupil teachers; (b) that the headmaster of the Secondary School be requested to submit to the committee a specimen set of questions for such examination, with a view to the same being submitted to H.M. Inspector for approval ; (c), that arrangements be made for the examination to be conducted by disinterested persons ; and (d), that the worked papers be marked by the headmaster of the Secondary School and be afterwards submitted to the committee and to H.M. "LIFE AND PERSONALITY OF WILLIAM HAZLITT."

iThe fourth of the series of University Extension Lectures on English essayists was delivered in the Co- operative Hall on Friday evening by the Bev. W. Law- rence Schroeder, M.A., the subject being " The life and 1 personality of William Hazlitt "—The lecturer com- menced by reading the tribute of Charles Lamb who 1 said that " William Hazlitt in his natural and healthy . state was one of the finest of spirits breathing." The man who could elicit from so keenly dis- criminating a soul as Lamb such regard and affection was worthy at least of their acquaintance if not intimacy. The Hazlitts claimed Ireland as the home of their ancestors. The idea of a Dutch origin was not worth the trouble of a possible verification. Hazlitt's father was a Unitarian minister who was sub- jected to the usual trials of a dissenting parson in those days. The lecturer briefly sketched the life of Hazlitt, touching upon the avidity with which at an early age he read what boys would now regard as heavy works, although he was one of the most active and happiest of boys. Mr. Birrell thought that Hazlitt was never is true Dissenter any more than he was a true democrat. Hazlitt's worship of Napoleon disturbed his (the lecturer's) idea of his democracy but of the reality of his Dissent there could not be a shadow of doubt. Intensity of application marked all that Hazlitt attempted. Under an impulse and feeling in himself some kind of power he decided to become a painter but after spending a great deal of time in the pursuit of art he was wise enough to take stock of his capacity and decided that painting as a profession was not for him. Straightway, with the genius of the strong man he turned his mind to literature and determined to be a writer. When we read flazlitt's essays we were tempted by reason of their lucidity to think them simple, but when we reflected we were bound to acknow- ledge that underneath them was an intellectual scheme, strong and virile in the best sense. De Quincey spoke of him as "An Ishmael—his hand against all men "and he (the lecturer) thought the term was appropriate. Hazlitt was not such a lovable man as Lamb, but there was something about him which evoked our pity end sympathy. He never seemed to have fitted in quite with the order of the universe—he was always at odds with the world. Never throughout the whole of his life was he in that close communion with friends which meant that he himself would realize the depths of his own heart. Most of his work was curt, crisp, and epigrammatic. He delighted in short sentences,/ and did not disdain personal references. •

div.head: "My DEAR CHILDREN,-_
div.p: "My DEAR CHILDREN,-_

Now that November is drawing to a close, I have made arrangements for our special Christmas Competition. I have been thinking a great deal as to how I can give a chance of a prize to all my members. Some of the younger ones may say that it is not much use sending in stories, etc., as the members with the advantage in age will be sure to carry off the prizes. This is right to a certain extent, but not entirely so. Each competition will have as prizes a very large and beautiful box of Fry's Chocolates, aid the second prizes will be handsome books. You must all observe the following rules in everything you send me : --ist : Age must be given on all con- tributions. 2nd: All contributions and answers trust reach the office of this paper not later than December 4th. 3rd: All letters and contribu- tions must be written on one side of the paper only, and as plainly as possible, as neatness will be taken into consideration. The following are the subjects :—ist : The best account of the happiest Christmas that you have spent. 2nd: The best short Christmas story. 3rd: Give an account of the original of Santa Claus. 4th: The best motto for the Children's Corner League for igo6.

The prize for correct answers has been sent this week to Freda Wellbourn. I was very pleased to receive photographs from Fred Cox. head, and I consider them very good. I also have to thank Leon Omm for a photo of himself and brother. I received numerous letters this week, but I can only publish the three best. I hope you will all show great interest in our Christmas Competitions, and remember for each subject given there is a first and second prize. With all good wishes, from UNCLE NED.

Dear Uncle Ned,—Thardc,you very much for your kind letter, but please do, not think I take no interest in the Children's Corner, for I do. I have tried to solve the puzzles every week, but have not succeeded with all of them. I could do two or three each week, but some I could not do at all, Besides, I am very busy indeed I am a pupil teacher, and have just commenced to go to the P.T. Centre at Newark. I go three days a week—Monday, Thursday, and Saturday. The other days I teach at Oxton, with half-a-day's holiday. When Igo to Newark, I start from home at 8 o'clock, and cycle five miles to the station. Then we go about 16 miles in the train, and leave Newark at four in the afternoon. I get home about a quarter past five, and then have a lot of home lessons to do. I like going to Newark very much indeed. It is not very nice cycling on a wet morning. I have just heard how I came out in my Scrip- ture Exam., which took place last September. came out second out of 41 P.T. candidates. I cannot write any more, for I have some history to learn. I did not see anything in this week's paper about the arrangement with Messrs. Hovis, but I will try with the puzzles, and write for one. We do not get the paper until Tuesday evening, but I send the puzzles off as soon as I possibly can. Now I must close, with best wishes for the success of the League. I like the motto very much, and I hope we shall all re- member it and act up to it. From your niece,

div.head: NELLIE PRATLEY.
div.p: NELLIE PRATLEY.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am very sorry I have not written to you before now, but I have had Such -.a number of home lessons lately that I have not had time for writing. I have read the Children's Corner League nearly every week, and have generally succeeded in solving the puzzles, although I have had no time to write them out. lam goinr, to write to-night rn 's Messrs. Hovis to get their puzzle, and try to solve it. So far, I think the puzzles have been very easy, and I have enjoyed reading the littic stories very nittch. I have a little sister called Kathleen. She is four years old, but she has gone away with mother to her grandma's, and has taken baby George With her. Father and I and Miss liallgarth are left at home by ourselves. We have a big garden, but it looks very bare just now, there being only a few chrysanthemums out. During the summer we had all kinds of flowers in it. The celery is just ready, and although it is small, it is Very nice. I have written the answers, to the puzzles on the other sheet of paper.—With best wishes, I remain, _
Yours sincerely, MARY G. 1V1L8).7.

Dear Uncle Ned,—Sorry I have not: written to you, but I have been busy at our shop. I am sending you a photo of my brother and my- self. You will see the difference in our char- acters. I am very fond of pets, and my brother iS more for soldiers. Round my little brother's shoulder is a Dutch bandolier, which by brother r Africa captured. It was not long, however, before the dogs and the lamb were on excellent terms. They seemed all at once to become great friends, and when the lamb was almost a full-grown sheep, it often forsook even Annie for ,the company of its new companions, and ran about everywhere with the dogs. Mr. Noble declared that he once heard the sheep trying to bark, but I am inclined to think he was making fun' of us. I can't be- lieve the lamb went so far as that, though no doubt it admired Rover's great loud " bow-wow " and felt that its own little " ba-a-a!" was, in comparison, very mild. The farmer often wished to take the sheep and kill it, now that it was too big for Annie to play with; but Mr. Noble declared that " Bob " —for so Annie had named it when it was a tiny baby—was one of the family, and that it should stay in, the yard with the dogs as long as it chose. One day I was in the snug library writing. It was the beginning of the cold weather, and a few days before there had been a heavy fall of snow—the first of the season—just the time when the wolves are often driven by hunger to attempt a raid on ' the farmers' poultry-yards.- Suddenly I heard a great commotion outside, and Tom and Harold ran past the window, shout- ing, "Rover, Jowlerhere, dogs! Wolf !--a wolf !"

I was putting my papers together, and think- ing whether I should venture out in the cold or whether I should leave them to catch the wolf by themselves, when Mr. Noble came in, saying, "Quick, Glaucus, quick! On with your coat! There is the funniest sight outside you ever saw." Of course I jumped up, hurried into my coat and •overshoes, and rushed out into the •snow, wondering what new feature there could be in the not unusual visit of a wolf to the farm, and when outside I saw the boys and dogs were running across the open clearing in full chase after two large wolves. But certainly there was the strangest sight I ever saw in my life! There among the pack of dogs ran •g Bob" scamper- ing along with the best of them, and "ba-a-a-ing " with all its might at the astonished wolves. I don't know what the sheep had planned to do if it caught them, but Bob's. actions were so threatening that we wondered whether it would have eaten a wolf for supper if it had overtaken one. Unluckily for our sport, however,' the wolves managed .to escape for that time, and Master Bob came home with the baffled pursuers, looking as proud as though it had sue- ceeded in securing some wolf for supper, and had enjoyed the taste. I don't know what became of Bob afterward, but I am convinced that a sheep with ambition enough to chase a wolf may have aspired to any- thing.

MUNICIPAL TEMPERANCE. Temperance advocates have often complained of the alleged, slow growth of the Temperance Movement nowadays, but sure!), the growth in Temperance sentiment in ordinary society is strikingly manifest. An example of how official bodies regard the drink evil is shown by the posters recently issued by the Camberwell and other borough Councils. In these the report by the Roy al Commission on Physical Deterioration are summarised; pointing out the evils of alcoholism and the benefits of abstinence. It would he well if local eunneils throughout the country would issue olllcial nr)!ices similar to this, end thqrn is a work for Free Churchmen to do to bring before the Municipal Autho- rities chub has been done in Camberwell.

Another case of sectarian persecution has just been revealed at Blackpool, where a child at a Roman Catholic School was beaten one Monday morning because it did not go to Sunday School the previous day. The affair was brought before the Board of Education, which "strongly disapproved of the action of the teacher." A promise has been made that such an affair shall not be repeated, but it is disgraceful that it should ever have been allowed to have happened.

div.head: NEXT NATIONAL COUNCIL.
div.p: NEXT NATIONAL COUNCIL.

Practically all the Free Church leaders have already consented to be present in Birmingham :luring the second week in March, 1906, when the annual gatherings of the National Free Church Council will be held. The programme is virtually completed, and it is anticipated that the assemblies in Birmingham will be of great interest. Great public meetings will be held thronghonfthe week in the Central Hall, where the sessions will he held, the, Town Hall, the Carr's-lane Chapel, all of which have been engaged for the week; and others will take place in nearly every town of any size through- out the Midlands, the number being probably about thirty. When the gathering was held in Birmingham it took the form of a Congress, the National Council not naving been formed on its present basis, and whereas there were then in azistence only 120 Free Church Councils—there are now 900.

div.head: GIPSY SMITH AT WESTAI/S3TER.
div.p: GIPSY SMITH AT WESTAI/S3TER.

Gipsy Smith, the well-known Evangelist, has just finished a great mission at Westminster Chapel, London. On the first Sunday of the mission, the huge building was packed and hundreds failed to gain admission. On Monday evening the audience included 600 blind people who sang alone a verse of the ever popular "Count your blessings." Dr. Campbell Morgan, minister of [the church, conducted a prayer meeting each morning in the chapel at inzht, and preached at one o'clock to business

and women, Gipsy Smith taking tme vening services. A pressing invitation has been sent to Gipsy Smith to conduct a serlea ef meetings in the United States. Arrangereents are being made for his visit there next year. He has toured the States two or three times before, and there is no doubt as to the reception he will receive. It is interesting to note that a volume of his addresses have just been published by the National Free Church Council under the title "As Jesus Passed By." The evangelist's many admirers will .doubtless produce a ready sale for the book.

div.head: REVIVAL SPREADING.
div.p: THE REVIVAL SPREADING.

The Rev. J. E. Roberts, MA., 8.D., has eontribrited a timely article to this month's Fiy.,! 'h,freknan on " Modern Revivals.- He says there are many tokens that the Revival is prAnding. "Perhaps a prison would he voted about the last place where a Revival is likely to appear. Yet God's Spirit has come to prisons, Sml has led hundreds of prisoners into the liberty of the glory of the children of God. This happened in Chatham Prison under the chaplaincy of Rev. Mr. Cobe. In his intense earnestness one morning he threw himself on his knees in front of the whole congrevation and invoked the power of the Divine Spirit to quicken the dead souls of the five hundred prisoners. The effect was electrical. Reckless of prison rules, more than a dozen men left their places and flung themselves on the ground in tears. From that day the prison was a changed institution. Equally remarkable was the result of the faithful work of Colonel Plummer, when he was appointed Governor of H.M. Prison. Parkhurst. Not long after his advent a spiritual wave broke over the place, and hundreds of criminals were converted."

div.head: MAGAZINE LOCALISING.
div.p: MAGAZINE LOCALISING.

A great many Free Churches and Free eihnrcts Councils are now considering the question of their localised magazine for 1906. The National Free Church Council. recognising the import- ance of the dissemination of good Free Church literature, issues the Free Churchnurn espe„Gially for the purpose of localising. Of recent years this magazine has increased its circulation by leaps and bonnds, the sales haying more than quadrupled in tbreeyears. An advance copy of the January number has been issued, and it would he dificilt to imagine a more suitable production for localising purposes. The publisher, National Free Church Council. Memorial Hall, London, E.C.. will send a copy of this, together with terms for localising, on application.

div.head: WESLEYAN PROGRESS.
div.p: WESLEYAN PROGRESS.

The WoslAyans have opened another great ion 11,01 in London, the Central Mission Ball at Plumstead. Lord and Lady 13rassey were present Lt the formal opening. The entire cost of the building, which includes a large central hall that will seat over 1500 persons, a smaller hall to seat 750, and numerous club and class-rooms. &e., was over £9I,CCO. which amount was fully provided for before the open- ing exercises were over. Rev. T. E. Westerdale is in charge of the mission. At the first Sunday's services both halls were crowded. and at the evening's meeting there were forty seeking salvation.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR
NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication mast in Rh cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith.

A Desirable Improvement. Sir,—Some months ago I, together with another resident in Latchford Ward, read with pleasure an article in the" Examiner" advocating the construction of a new road from Latchford to Wilderspool. Shortly after the publication of that article the site for the road was fenced off and the work of laying out the road commenced,but to the surprise of all the work has ceased. The opening of the road would effect a desir- able improvement and by making a short cut from Wilderspool to Latchford would relieve a large amount of traffic which at present has to go via Warrington Bridge. I would like to know why the road has not been completed. Surely the Corporation do not want more than has already been given them—the value of which I place at £5OOO. I understand that if the work is not put in hand the offer will be withdrawn and the ratepayers will have to pay heavily for what is now offered to them free of cost. I trust this urgently- needed improvement will have the immediate attention of the members of the Town Council.—Yours, DISGUSTED RATEPAYER.

The Ragged School and Mission. S iT,—Perrn it me through your columns to thank the many friE-mls who have hitherto assisted us in our attempt to ameliorate the conditions under which Warrington's poorest children take their part in what is too often a real "struggle for existence.' The approach of the Christmas season will bring the usual round of appeals to all, and we hope the case of the Ragged School children will not be overlooked in the many other calls made on public generosity. The report we issue shows that we have many kind supporters in the town, and we hope this year to increase the number. Our helpers will make their usual Christmas rounds but there are many who sympathise with the work whom we have not yet reached. If any such friends will send a postcard to the Ragged School we shall be glad to include them in our list of calls. Our appeal at this season is not only for funds, but also for food, clothing, toys, books, S:c. (new and old)— anything in fact that will help to brighten the lot of those who are unable to help themselves. With thanks to our old supporters, and to you, Sir,for space for this appeal, yours &c., for the Committee, ALFRED HULME (Hon. Sec.) November 22nd, 1905.

div.head: MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.
div.p: THE MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.
" King Olaf."

The Musical Society opened its season on Wednes- day with a good concert, but a poor audience. In response, we understand, to some expressed desire, the presentation of Sir Edward Elgar's "King Olaf" was for a second time undertaken, after an interval of only a year and nine months. The performance of this early work of the composer's was, it will be remembered, on the first occasion, greeted by the audience with a degree of interest and enthusiasm which seemed to hold out some justification for its early repetition. Such hopes as seemed to be thus promised of a warmer public welcome, were however strangely disappointed in the cooler reception accorded to the work on Wednesday, a circumstance which it is difficult to explain, for its performance then was freer from serious defect than the first, being in fact in all essentials adequate, and therefore highly satisfactory. The society's vocal members had a difficult task in dealing with the "King Olaf" score, the difficulties -arising chiefly from the complex interweaving of the choral rarts with passages for the principal voices, I and in the necessity of often declaiming these in a I manner which, while wholly convineing, must often be , characterised by great restraint. Ic was not however ' in these parts so much as in straightforward places that uncertainties were sometimes manifest in the singing of the chorus. What excuse for instance can be offered for so weak a commencement by the female voices in the chorus "Sigrid sits in her high abode"? The more solid choral numbers such as "The challenge of Thor," "The Wraith of Odin" and "The death of Olaf," were splendidly presented, a sense of massiveness and dramatic power being conveyed to the listener which indicated a most intelligent insight into the composer's meaning as well as most conscientious work done in the rehearsals. There were also highly praiseworthy choral presentments of a more dainty order, of which "A little bird in the air " and that unaccompanied portion of the Epilogue commencing " As torrents in summer" are two of many beautiful instances. The parts for the principal voices were in the safe hands of Madame Clementine de Vere, Mr. Alfred Heather and Mr. Charles Knowles. The important duet between the first and second, which forms a luminous centre of interest in the composer's tone picture, received a finely emotional interpretation. Mr. Knowles is especially to be congratulated on his forceful and dramatic rendering of some telling passages in the Thor music and in the solos of Ironbeard. The work of the orchestra may be • alluded to in terms of unstinted praise. " King Olaf " makes most exigent demands upon the whole body of instrumentalists, and though in no spirit of hypercriticism it might be said that the orchestration was occasionally somewhat overwhelm- ing, it must be admitted that a ready response to the conductor's baton and a due subserviency to the voice parts was generally manifested. The repletion of instruments requisitioned by the composer's score rendered it necessary to largely reinforce the society's bandsmen, the whole performance thereby gaining a completeness which is highly' creditable to the society's management. Preceding the choral work the " Peer Gynt " suite was played by this augmented orchestra with such success that in the climax of the final movement the audience were roused to such a pitch as to make its repetition imperative.

div.head: WARRINGTON BAND OF HOPE UNION.
div.p: WARRINGTON BAND OF HOPE UNION.
Gathering at the Winroarleigh Cafe.

The Warrington Band of Hope Union is in a very flourishing condition, and evidence of its power for usefulness and good in the town was afforded on Thurs- day evening. At the invitation of the President, Mr. R. A. Naylor and Miss Naylor, the members held a social gathering at the Winmarleigh Caf+3, and spent a highly enjoyable evening. Some two hundred invita- tions had been issued, and the majority of the recipients availed themselves of the opportunity of partaking of Mr. Naylor's hospitality. The HosT occupied the chair and in a brief speech advocated moderation in the fight to overcome the evils of drink. In some quarters, be said, temperance people had a bad name, end he had been told it would be an advantage if they were a little more sincere in their words, looks and actions. From their standpoint a diminution or an entire removal of licences would be a good thing, yet they sometimes failed to grasp the fact that unfortunately they formed only about 20 per cent, of the total population of the country. They could not go to the remaining 80 per cent, and say We will force you by legislation to adopt our principles." He did not know whether they would agree but he thought it did not do any good to the temperance movement to deal harshly with those connected with what was a very difficult and trying business of supplying the wants of that portion of the population who demanded a means of buying intoxicants. Being a minority the majority would rebel if they tried to do such a thing and in his opinion such a course would multiply the foes of temperance instead of increasing the number of their friends. (Hear,hear.) The Band of Hope was the real direction in which they should apply their energies, and, in the words of the wise man, if they could only persuade the children Awalk in the ways of temperance they would not art from them. He hoped the Band of Hope workers /in Warrington would rally round the old flag and if they were perfectly true and real in their endeavours Providence would be sure to bless their labours. (Applause.) Mr. CHANDOS WILSON, secretary of the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope Union delivered a stirring address. They were engaged, he said not so much in curing the intemperance of the present but in preventing intemperance in the future. He emphasised the need of thoroughness in the work. ( Applause.) During the evening an excellent musical programme was submitted by the Misses A. Woodland and E. Woodland, and Messrs. Phillips and Spruce who dis- played considerable ability in solos, duets and quartettes. On the motion of the Rev. H. DUNNICO seconded by the Rev. J. S. HUGHES Mr. Naylor, Mr. Wilson and the artistes were heartily thanked for their services. A similar compliment was paid to Mr. Gandy for his work as secretary of the Union. Refreshments were served and the remainder of the evening was spent in a social manner.
