THE FINANCIAL POSITION. The treasurer (Mr. F. Most(s) reported as follows In presenting the statement of accounts for the past year, I am sorry to say the debit balance has increased from £25 10s. 10d. to £lBO Os. 3d. a loss on the year of £l5l 15s, sd. For the information of the subscribers 1 have drawn up a statement showing the work of the Society for the past eight years :—Total number of cases nursed, 3,140 ' • total number of visits paid,1.18,952; total income from all sources, £1,052 16s. lid. ; total expenditure for maintenance and salaries,£3,Bs7 18s. Bd.; total expenditure for furnishing and alterations, £375 4s. Gd. ; leaving an adverse balance for the eight years of £lBO Gs. 3d. There are unpaid accounts of £l7 13s. 9d. making a total of £l9B Os. In addition there is a balance of £251 16s. 6d. due for the purchase of the INurses' Home. If the work is to be continued on the present scale which is inadequate to meet the require- ments of the Town, we shall have to make some effort to liquidate the debt. DEBT ON THE HOME CLEARED OFF. 1 The CHAIRMAN said he was glad to inform the meeting that through the liberality of friends he had been able to get sufficient money to clear off the debt on the nurses' home. (Applause.) The donors were : Mr. Vere B. Davies, £200; Mr. Leonard Davies, £200; Mr. Edward Davies, £2OO (as a memorial to their late father and mother) ; Mrs. Thomas. of Swansea, £5O; Mr. Henry Thornton, £5O; Mr. William Long, £5O ; The Co-operative Society, £5O ; Monks, Hall and Com- pany, £5O: Joseph Crosfleld and Sons, Ltd., £3O; Peter Walker and Sons, Ltd., £25; Greenall, Whitley and Co.. Ltd., £25 ' Lady Greenall, £2O; Mrs. John Cros- field, £2O ; Alderman Smethurst, £5; Colonel Buckton, £5 • making a total of £9BO. The debt on the home was 296"1165. 6d., and it was intended to spend a few more pounds on a tablet, but the donations he had received would clear off the whole amount. (Applause.) He had written to several other people in the neighbourhood but his appeal had met with a rather poor response. He had also written to another gentleman whom he hoped might help them, because he was not unwilling to help at building organs and so on, and he (the Chair- man) thought he could not do better than send that Association a little towards paying off its debt. (Hear, hear.) It was also decided to have a workingmen's committee, and he believed there was a gentleman present (Mr. C. H. Newtoa) who was willing to act as secretary. THE CONGREGATIONAL COLLECTIONS. In moving the adoption of the reports the Rector expressed delight that the debt on the home had been cleared offand he was sure that it must bring joy to the chairman's heart and to all who were interested in the institution. He was pleased to notice an Increase—a very small one it'wasltrue—in the subscriptions and con- gregational collections which amounted to £266 as against £2OO. With regard to the congregational collections they had risen from £3O to £4O, including the Parish Church offertory which came in too late to be reckoned in this year's account. He was sorry to see that public donations had decreased from £l3O to £lOO and working men's contributions from £6O to £3O. He saw there was a similar decrease with respect to the Infirmary and he had no doubt it was to be accounted for by the want of work for he was sure the working man appreciated both institu- ions. It was also to be regretted that the income for the year had decreased from £5OO to £450 and the result was the deficit of £2OO exclusive of the cost of the home He wanted to commend most earnestly to everyone the splendid work of the institution. In the eight years of its existence 120,000 visits to patients had bsen paid and during the last veer alone the visits numbered 20,000. He noticed tlat 500 cases had been cured or relieved and a highfy satisfactory feature was that 350 of the 500 cases had been sent in by medical inenAN hen the institution was founded he believed the medical men looked a little askance at it, and he did not wonder as they thought there might be interference. They had now, however, learnt to appreciate the value of the nurses' work. He would like to ask that offertories should be taken at all places of worship on behalf of the Association. It was sad that in a large town like War- rington with a population of nearly 70,000 the congrega- tional collections should be from £3O to £lO. The Rector concluded by expressing his appreciation of the liberality of Mr. Monks and his family towards the institution.

On a chilly wet Thursday evening a few weeks ago, I set out, with a feeling of great virtue at leaving a ; comfortable fire and pleasant company, to visit the I Girls' Club in Silver-street. After wandering down Winwick-road, and crossing a terribly muddy play- ground, which somewhat damped my ardour as well ' as my boots, I was directed to the door by a couple of grinning urchins Who seemed to have very highly developed that sense of humour which sees something exquisitely funny in other people's mishaps They had watched my splashing progress with great relish. Passing through an empty room, I opened the d of another and found a group of twenty or thirty.girls gathered round a roaring fire with the matron in the centre. They all stood up as I entered—a mark of respect which is apt to be embarrassing to an unpre- pared visitor, particularly as you feel you are being weighed, and perhaps found wanting at the same time. There were girls of any age from 16 upwards, and some of them didn't look that, bat though they might be small, they were not lacking in , other respects. Their costume varied, but as regards coiffure, what someone has called "fire-irons " seemed to be de riquele. ,One wonders on what gala day those curling-pins are unloosed, and if it is possible to get a comb through the frizziness , resulting, which must rival that of a negro. As Thursday is the " play night" of the week, the girls were allowed to do pretty much as they liked, and those who had talent were encouraged to show it. It isn't lacking either, as anyaae would agree, who once saw the " cake-walk " danced by some of the members, who rumour sars, practise on Saturday nights at thie foot of School Brow to the strains of a barrel organ. Then there are soloists of some merit, while in unison the club will sing anything from hymns to a popular ditty called "Angeline." If a member is known to be I able to sing, or recite, and shows any reluctance in I coming forward, she is promptly seized, and pushed I into the arena, by those nearest to her. If she falters in her performance there is always someone ready to ' prompt, and she is sure of a round of applause at the end. Occasionally they are interrupted ;by a scuffle and chuckle at the closed door, which one of the girls explained as caused by "them lads," and showed an evident willingness to go out and " settle " them, which had to be restrained. - -

_ It seems a pity if the boys haven't something of the same kind to Interest them. Pethaps they have. Otherwise it must be rather tantalising to hear the sounds of " bobble and revel" awl not be able to jOin in. As it was getting near 9 o'clock, the closing hour, we had a game or two to finish with. It is no trouble to teach 'Silver-street" a new game; they are very quick at grasping ideas and if there is a some- what prominent part to be taken the difficulty is --not to find someone to take it —but to persuade half-a-dozen others that only one is necessary. At nine, the girls leave the glowing fire, with some reluctance, and go home. It doesn't take them long to put their things on. A shawl depends for its effect or artistic draping. You just put it on your head, and then throw one end over the left shoulder with a careless swing. Thus robed the Girls' Club vanished in twos and threes, into the night.

The Rev. C. HARVEY COOK seconded. He, too, believed that the lack of employment affected the amount of the contributions and the committee must not lose heart, especially considering that the debt on the home was now extinguished.
The report was adopted. it was decided to elect Mr. C. H. Newton as a mem- ber of the committee in order that he may act as secretary to the proposed workingmen's ,iommittee.

THE NURSES THANKED. The Rev.Jotts YONGE moved a cordial vote of thanks Ito Miss Whitfield (superintendent) and the staff of nurses for their devoted services daring the year. Ile I I said that was one of those happy occasions when many r of them could meet together and share in the work who were not always accustomed to act on the same lines. It was one of the happy features of both the Infirmaryl and the Nursing Association that they brought together all kinds of people in harmony in works of Christian I philanthropy. Mr. Yonge referred in terms of the highest praise to the work of the nurses 'pointing out that in May the number of I visits paid by the nurses averaged 13 distinct cases each per day. They pursued their visits from 8.30 in the morning to 1.30 and from 5 to 8, although that time was not rigidly kept, and in many cases it was considerably exceeded. He was pleased to be able to state that the Corporation bad shown an interest in the Institution by allowing the nurses the free use of the tram cars. (Applause.) Mr. Yonge referred to the work of the nurses and to the character of some of the homes they had to visit. He said they must have to encounter some of the most unpleasant atmospheres and attend to the requirements of obnoxiotts and painful cases. They had also to deal with the ignorance and helplessness of many of the poorer people, and all these things com- bined to make the work hard and wearing. He was glad that the confidence of the doctors of the town in the Institute seemed to be increasing if they were to judge by the number of cases sent in, and in passing the resolu- tion he could assure the nurses that it was not ' formally done, but was an expression of their honest sympathy, their intelligent sympathy,and as people who entered to the best of their ability into the experience into which those sisters of their's went from day to day As a matter of fact the nurses were doing what was really the work of all, because if he understood the spirit of the Gospel ef Jesus Christ at all, it taught them that the master intended His diciples, no matter what their name or creed might be, to care for those who are needy, and in distre,s and to minister to those who were sick. (Applause). Therefore the nurses were really carrying out the work which the great Master had pit into the hands of every one of them who pro- fessed to be His followers and servants. (Applause). Mr. J. RYMER YorNo seconded, and endorsed all the proposer of the resolution had said. He was sure no institution had a warmer place in the hearts of the tcoanspeople, and the noble work done by the nurses deserved the most cordial recognition. ([Tear, hear.) A working man whose family had received benefit from the nurses added his tribute to their worth. The CHATRNIAN said they could not say too much in praise of Miss Whitfield and her staff, and he was sorry they did not receive the financial support to enable them to keep one or two additional nurses. div.head: JUNIOR LIBERAL LEAGUE.
div.p: JUNIOR LIBERAL LEAGUE.
"John Knox and Scottish Political History."

The third weekly meetinr, of the Warrington Junior Liberal League was held at Gregory's Cafe on Monday evening, when an address was delivered by the Rev.J.L. Milne on "John Knox, with reference to Scottish Political History." Mr. Adams presided over a good attendance.

The LECTURER dealt in an able and interesting manner with his subject. He briefly illustrated the sad state of affairs in Scotland in 1505—the year of Knox's birth—especially with regard to the malpractices in the Roman Church. He sketched the career of the great reformer, his trials and his alsolute fearlessness. Continuing he said, some 3people argued that ministers should not interfere with politics, but what of Knox and the other reformers, and what of the prophets of old who were as much politicians as preachers of the Word of God? Be (Mr. Milne) agreed that a minister had no right to attempt to thrust his politics down his people's throats, using the pulpit for that end. But what was .neant by the word politics? What did the term include? If the Chinese slavery question and the Education Bill and the Brewers' Bill were within the scope of politics the minister's duty was plain. The right or wrong of any action, whether of the individual or State, was his affair. Speaking generally, for Government in the abstract Knox had the profoundest reverence, but the Govern- ment must be good if he supported it. Knox did not forget the people. He did not flatter them. He was no democrat, and he spoke rather of the " rascal multi- tude," but his education system proved that he did not forget them. He (the speaker) was travelling near Oxford at the time el the South African war, and at one of the stations an elderly man entered his compartment and asked the news of the war. He (the speaker) offered him a paper, but the man could not read. That was near Oxford, the great centre of education; but that man was poor and knowledge was not for him. A paragraph was sometimes seen in the papers with a heading "From Board School to University," as it was such an uncommon occurence for a Board school lad to pass through the University. In the land of Knox lads by the hundreds entered the University every year. The Universities were for all and open to all, rich and poor, if they bad the strength and pluck. The facilities wets so great as compared with England ; the doors were open so wide, thanks to the work of John Knox. And Mr. Carnegie by his munificence had made it more possible still. The universities in Scotland, thanks to Mr. Carnegie's munificence, were now as free as the day schools. He (Mr. Milne) knew that some did not like that. It was better, they said, when the young worked and studied and took the University course. Knox would have parish schools everywhere and secular control and he would have education compulsory. Wit h reference to the revenue of the Disestablished Church,'Knox would have it applied:to education, but in that he was baffled by the nobles, who hastened to divide the spoil. Two parts of the money, Knox said bitterly, was freely given to the Devil and the third part was divided between God and the Devil. (Applause). An interesting discussion followed. Mr. Hanoin GRAY argnad that it was essential that we should have a nationalized secular training for all children. The education question was a very difficult one and the adoption of a secular system seemed the only solntion of the difficulty. (Hear, hear). Others who took part in the discussion were Mr. J. Hawthorn, Mr. Adams, Mr. Morral and Mr. J. L. Hawthorn. A vote of thanks to the speaker and the chairman concluded tho meeting.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
[By " Ovallst."l

It will bs good news to Warringtonians that negotia- tions have practically been competed for the transfer of Arthur Widdeson, the one-time crack wing three- quarters of Broughton Rangers to Warrington. For two seasons the little Broughton man has been at loggerheads with the Rangers and as a result hi football playing has been confined to the juniors. Pendleton Brittania is the name of the club he has been assisting, but he is also on the professional register for ehadderton. Since the injury to Fish, Warrington have been trying hard to secure the transfer of Widdeson who, if he has retained his foroa will be a valuable capture.

I To-day's match is with Swintoa, away and War- rington mean to make a strong effort to repeat their fine performance at the colliery village a season ago. Widdeson has been placed on the left wing, with ' Isherwood, and the selected fifteen should be quite the equal of anything the Blues can pat in the field. The team is expected to be : Hallam, full back ; Widde- son, Isherwood, Brooks and Harris, three-quarters ; Hockenhall and J. Davies, half backs; Prestou. Board- man, Heath, Swift, Thomis, Shugars, Balton, and Cook, forwards. The League table up-to-date is as follows : For. Agst. Per-

Another new man has been signed on by Warrington this week, in the person of Owen Jones, a young centre three-quarter from the Runcorn Junior League. Jones has been much sought after, and the Warrington officials are confident they have made a good capture. He is very well-built, and will assist the " A. ' team to-day.

Last Saturday, the " A " to nu had waters all thsir own way in the friendly mutch with Stlford A.delphi. The latter made a very brave start, but died away rapidly later on and were finally defeated by 33 points to nil. To-day the Juniors have more serious work in their Competition fixture with Chaddertoa. It will be remembered that they only just won on the Chadder- ton ground by a goal to nil. The selected team is :C, Ashton, full-back ;.-Ksayan, Jones, Jordin aad Knight, threevarters ,; Garside and Lloyd, half-bucks; H trtley. Forster, Fairhurst, Elijah Lunt, and Harmer, for ivards.

Two of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Cup semi- finals have had to be re-played this week, and as a result Hunslet easily vanquished Hull Kingston lovers and Leigh defeated Widnes after a hard game. The finals will now be played between Halifax and Hunslot in Yorkshire, and Wigan and Leigh it Lincashire. Both should provide rare struggles, bat not much classy football.

div.head: Hockey.
div.p: Hockey.

The return match between Stockton Heath and Latch- ford drew quite a crowd to the Arpley ground on Satur- day. Stockton Heath had made no secret of the fact that they meant to reverse the defeat sustained at Latchford, and a keen game vias expected. Expecte- Mims were fully realised too, for neither side gave any- thing, away, and the Heathens finally triumphed by 3 goals to 1. From start to finish play was very fast and full of good hockey. There was very little body play and few penalties, and considering the local rivalry the game was contested in an excellent spirit. There is no questioning the superiority of the Heathens this time, though Latchford had a good share of the game and scored first. Their methods have not quite the same polish as those of the Stockton Heath men, and the latter justified their claim to be the cleverer side.

Among individuals Kirkconnel was the shining-light and gave an excellent display at centre half, frequently getting the better of the dashing Latchford forwards. W. Richardson was very smart and scored the best of the three goals, 1. Pierpoint getting the other two. At back the skipper, E. Pierpoint was steady as a rock. On the Latchford side, Hallows, Cli tfe, Spenceley and IV. Knight all distinguished themselves in some fast play.

Warrington hockey enthusiasts will shortly have the opportunity of seeing a county match, as the Stockton Heath ground (Arplev Cricket Ground) has been chosen for the Cheshire v. Westmorland match which is to be played on December 2nd.

Cheshire have chosen a very strong side, and although I have not been able to get hold of the names of all the players who are chosen in time for these notes, it will be enough to mention that Peel, Draper and Totlow are included in the side.
Last week I had the pleasure of mentioning that L. Fairclough had been chosen as reserve right back for Cheshire in their match versus Lincoln, and E. Pierpoint has now been chosen reserve loft back.

Latchford A and Stockton Heath A played their return match at Latchford on Saturday and it resulted in a win for the home team by two goals to nil. Stockton Heath pressed hard and played with surprising dash in the first ton minutes, but the home defence proved sound. Then Latchford recovered, and scored, this proving to be the only goal up to half time. They kept up the pressure in the second half and scored again, Warburton and Cobb being the scorers.

This Saturday, the 25th, Latchford play Eccles at Latchford, the team being : W. Unsworth, goal ;IL Hallows and T. Dixon, full-backs ; W Knight, J. B. Wilkinson, and A. H. Rathhone, half-backs ; W. H. Spensley, E. F. Chile, D. Knight, .1. Callan and .1. K. Conway, forwards. Bully-off, 2.45.

WIRRAL AND BTRIOENHEAD SHOW FOR 1906.- CHANGE OF DATES.

In consequence of the Staffordshire also the Lincoln- shire Agricultural Society having selected the 18th and 19th July for their 1906 show prior to this Society arranging for the same dates, it has now been decided to hold this Society's Show a week later than previously announced, viz. on Wednesday 25th and Thursday 26th July.

div.head: LABOUR PARTY AND THE RECENT ELECTIONS.
div.p: LABOUR PARTY AND THE RECENT ELECTIONS.
MR. PLINSTON'S REASON FOR RETIREMENT. An Eleventh Hour Discovery. HEATED DISCUSSION iT THE TRADES COUNCIL.

IA heated discussion occurred at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council which was held on Tuesday evening, upon the position of Mr. Edwin Plinston with regard to the recent municipal ! elections in Warringtou. The debate was opened by Mr. Smith who raised a question upon the following minute of the previous meeting which was read by the I secretary. "It was reported by the delegates to the Labour Representation Committee that Mr. Edwin Plinston' the nominee of the Trades Council had been selected to represent the committee and to contest Bewsey Ward." Mr. PLUMB presided over a good attendance. Mr. SMITII asked why, in face of the report, Mr. Plinston had withdrawn his candidature. The CHAIRMAN ruled Mr. Smith out of order as the subject would not be open for discussion until a later stage in the proceedings. Mr. SMITH : I have a right to speak. I want justice and insist upon having justice. I mean to ask some very severe questions upon trade union points. The Cieeritmee : I will see that you have justice and that you get all the information which it is possible to give you. Mr. SMITH : I move that the minutes be rescinded. Mr. Grefetee : I second that for the sake of the fun. Mr. BULLOCK : I take it that Mr. Smith wants an explanation. One will have to be given him in due Course. Mr. GREALY : The question is this. Mr. Plinston was Approved by this Council and also by the Labour Representation Committee, and then Councillor Stott wrote a letter saying he could not support him. Councillor STOTT : It is a question of procedure. Nothing will be kept back. If we rescind the minute we rescind something which the Labour Representation Committee has done. Mr. GREA.LEY : We nominate is man and then the secretary opposes him. That is rather inconsistent. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Ser ern withdrew his amendment and the minutes were approved. The Seceemitv read a letter from Mr. 0. Buckley, secretary of the Warrineton Labour Representation Committee in which he said : "It was found that Mr. , Plinston's candidature was in conflict with rule 6, clause 3 of the constitution of the committee and upon this being pointed out to Mr.Plinston he decided to retire. The committee regret that the municipal elections have passed without haying secured another representative on the Town Council." ' Mr. BUCKLEY said he had nothing further to add to I his letter. I Mr. litooremorroal, representative of the Trades Council on the Labour Representation Committee, said ,he felt very keenly on the matter. He went to the committee meeting thinking he had at the back of him the support of the Trades Council. He did not know why the special meeting was called and to his surprise the first intimation he received that anything was wrong was the reading of a letter from Councillor Stott, in consequenee of which Mr. Plinston decided to resign. They had endorsed his candidature and yet the secretary of the Trades Council repudiated him. What he learnt I at the meeting of the Labour Representation Committee must have been known when they endorsed Mr. Plinston's candidature. (A VOICE : " Question "). Mr. Hyrciles : There seems to be something very I fishy about this. When it was found that Mr. Plinston I was not acceptable to the Labour Representation Com.l mittee a special meeting of this Council should hwe been called for the purpose of adopting him as a candidate. It appears as though we are to be ruled by the Labour Representation Committee. Mr. BUCKLEY: We are affiliated .to the Labour Representation Committee awl send delegates to repro- sent us and have no more right to attempt to dictate; to the committee than any other Society repro- I seated. If the Labour Representation Com- mittee found something wrong with Mr. Plinston's candidature they bad a perfect right to withdraw his name without consulting the Trades Council. It is for the Labour Representetina Committee to judge what is ' right according to their rules. Rule 6, clamse 3 reads "All candidates will be required to sever their connec- tion with any political party, either Liberal or Tory ?" Hircfree: Mr. Plinston was drawn in front of the Independent Labour Party. Tee CH AMU AN: Teat is not tree. A circular was snot by Mr. Plinston with the Independent Labour Party and he was invited to attend before the com- mittee. I object to the statement that he was drawn. Mr. SMITH: Sseiug that we nominated Mr. Plinston we should have been prepared to fight for him almost to a man. T was willing to support him. Mr. BUCKLEY ; But you did not do so. Mr. SMITH : Mr. Plinston is the ablest man we can get and here the Labour Representation Committee scorn him and throw him overboard. Mr. BUCKLEY : Nothing of the sort. The CHAIRMAN : I cannot allow that sort of language. Mr. SMITFI : I am going to say whet I have to say. Mr. BUCKLRY : No one his scorned him. Mr. Set ITfl : Oh yes they have. Apparently we have no right to expect the Labour Representation Com- mittee to consider our nomination. Mr. PODMORE : This Council decided to ally them- selves with the Labour Representation Committee, and have to accept the deeisioes of the Lie° le R3prnianta- tion Committee. If you are not satisfied you will have to move and we secede. Mr. Gee.% LEV : How many were present when Mr Plinston was overthrown? Mr. BUCKLEY : IFs was not overthrown. He retired. Mr. GREALEY : lie was asked to retire. Mr. Feueexert : When Mr. Pliusten NV LS adopted by the COMMittee as a candidate, was it known that he was in couflict with rule 6 ? Mr. Bueicr.ev : No. I have only to refer to Mr. Plinston's statements when he Was adopted to show that we did not know he was in conflict with the rules. We found that out afterwards. When it WAS discovered it was pointed out to Mr. Plinston and he was asked to put himself in conformity with the Jules. He decided to retire. Mr. [DOG INBOTTOM thought that when the Labour Representation Committee failed Mr. Plinston, the Trades Council should have run him themselves. The CHAIRMAN : We cannot run candidates so long as we are affiliated with the Labour Representation Committee. Mr. HITCFIEN : Then I give notice that I will move that we secede from the Labour Representation Committee. Councillor STOTC: Wd joined the Labour Repro- tation Committee because a number of the members of the Council do not believe ia taking political action. The Labour Representation Committee exists for politi- cal purposes and therefore we decided to join. Mr. Plinston was adopted by the Committe and was invited to attend before the com- mittee. A number of questions were put to him with regard to his position in connection with a certain political party in Warrington and from the replies which he gav6 he led us to believe that he was not in any way connected with the Liberal party. He satisfied the whole of the delegates present and I can assure you he was given some stiff questions to answer. I Was fully prepared to support him. A paragraph appeared in the Examiner " and ins reply to the criticisms of that Mr. Plinston made statements which made us more convinced that his position was perfectly straightforward and was perfectly ill accord with the Labour Representation Committee constitution. What surprises me is that Mr. Smith and Mr. Hitchen should come here and complain of Mr. Plinston]being snubbed when they had had a Crest dell to say against his candi- dature and in support of Mr. Peacock. Mr. [Mohan , certainly said after the last meeting, after Mr. Plinston had been spelking, that he (Mr. Plinston) was telling deliberate untruths with regard to his connection with I the Liberal party and gave certain informetion with regard to Mr. Plinston's position in the Liberal party Now he wants the Trades Council to believe that Mr Plinston has been snubbed by the Labour Representation I Committee. I like honesty and so far as I arn concerned I will be honest. Another paragraph appeared in the 1" Examiner " which criticised what Mr. Plinston had , said. A circular was next received by the Indepen- dent' Labour Party asking them if they would I receive Mr. Plinston and hear his views upon labour matters. lie atteneed before the committee of the Labour Party and a rather warm meeting was I held. Mr. Plinston was asked certain questions and from his answers I was convinced that he could not be nominated :LS a Labour Representation Committee I candidate, as he could not run in accordance with the constitution of the Committee. fis acknowledged that he was still a member of the Liberal Party and had attended recent meetings of the party. The Labour Representation Committee were not aware of this or they would never have accepted him, until he had put himself in agreement with the constitution of the committee. If Mr. Plinston had at the outset officially resigned his connection with the Liberal Party, no in atter wn it the " 1!;•( toli nor " or any one else said, he would have brought himself in line with the rules of the Labour Representation Committee and could have been run as a Labour Representation Committee candidate. Had he done so I would have given him my support. So long as he was connected with the Liberal Party, was it likely that L who have been fighting for 12 years for independent labour repre- sentation, was going to support his candidature? No one can deny his ability, but before I would have sup- ported his candidature I would have resigned, and I am prepared now to resign my position as secretary of the Trades Council, if the Council think I acted wrongly. I hope Mr. Plinston will not take anything I say as personal, but I am bound to speak in reply to Mr. Ifigginbottom. Prior to my obtaining that information it was the Independent Labour Party and the Socialists who were supporting Mr. Plinston, and not certain mem-

div.head: BEAUTIFYING STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: BEAUTIFYING STOCKTON HEATH.
Successful hauguratiou of the Scheme.

The scheme for the beautifying of Stockton Heath has aroused great enthusiasm in the district. The originators of the idea hoped that they might awaken a desire to make the village more attractive but the response to their appeal for assistance in carrying out the object exceeded the expectations of even the most sanguine. The first step was taken on Saturday when, what will in the future be known as the planting day, was inaugurated. rtv, responsible committee had hoped to be able to plant twelve trees this year hut they had greatly underestimated the interest taken in the proposal and almost ten times that number of plants were placed at their disposal. The selection of the 'sites for the trees has not been carried out in-Used min- ately but upon an organized and pre-arranged plan which promises to give the greatest satisfaction. The first tree to be planted was placed opposite the police station by Mrs. H. V. Pigot, who was asked to perform the ' ceremony as the wife of the fist president of the Garden Society—the original movers in the matter. The proceedings attracted a large gathering over which ' Mr. Vera B. Davies,. president of the Garden Society, presided. The Chairman explained that the object of the move- ment was not confined to the encouraging of the plant- ing of trees but was also to promote the provision of window boxes, creepers, and generally to introduce I householders to take a greater interest in their gardens. The movement had hada very encouraging start and he I hoped that in years to come the inhabitants of the dis- trict would take such an interest in the movement that a special society would not be needed. (Applause.) Mrs. PIGOT then amidst applause planted the first tree and the speech making was resumed. Mr. Boum-Hut, who spoke as chairman of the Parish Council, said the interest and sympathy of the members of the Council had been shown by the fact that they had all sub=cribed largely to the movement. He thought the committee were to be congratulated upon the splendid success which had attended their efforts. (Applause.) He thought there was one splendid feature of the scheme which was that they had asked the school children to subscribe for is tree. An educa- tion iu the sense of the beautiful was as important as education in the direction of the three We. If they helped to cultivate a sense of the beautiful in children they helped to do something which would have a good influence upon their future. (Applause.) They would he helping social reformers, temperance advocates and ministers or religion as they would induce the children to regard life from a different and higher standpoint than would, probably, otherwise be the cane. (Hear, hear.) They had begun well but there remained a great deal to be done and there must be no relaßation of effort on the part of everyone concerned to do every- thing that could be done to beautify the village in the directions indicated by the Chairman. (Applause.) Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins expressed hi a pleasure at the enthusiasm which had been displayed, which he hoped would continue to be shown. (Hear, hoar). Mr.J. H. Clarke'pointed to the avenue of trees in Grappenhall road as evidence of the improvement which could he effected by the planting of trees. Helwas very pleased to see that the children had taken up the question with such enthusiasm—(hear, hear)—an enthusiasm which he thought would have a tendency to induce them to take an interest in the growth of the trees and to see that they were not ill-used. (Applause). The Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson, who spoke as president of the Beautiful Warrington Society, said they all knew th 3 object of the Society which he represented, was to make Warrington as beautiful as they possibly could. Conse- quently the members of the Society looked with the greatest possible sympathy noon the kindred movement which was going on in Stockton Heath, and which had been so auspiciously inaugurated. He could net hello thinking when he crossed the Ship Canal, that by the planting of trees and shrubs on its banks, they conic' make the canal an object of extreme beauty. In several places on the banks there was an excellent growth of the yellow broom, and all they had to do was to encour- age and further the movement which nature had taken up. (Bear, hear.) lie was sure the members of the Warrington Society most cordially wished them a great and lasting success in the movement which they had begun that day. (Applause.) Mr. Edward Wallington also expressed his interest and sympathy in the movement. Mr. H. J. Westbrook said they had set their hands to a good work and yet it seemed to him that they were only doing their duty. Trees not only made the district beautiful but they sorted a more useful purpose as"thev were sanitary agents more persistent than any public officer of health." He moved a vote of thanks to Mrs. Pigot for her services. (Applause). Mr. W. H. Woodcock seconded and the vote was heartily accorded. The Rev. H. V. Pigot briefly responded. On the motion of Mr. C., Plinston, seconded by Dr. Parker, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. V. B. Davies for presiding. The business of the afternoon was then proceeded with the following planting trees :—Mrs. Pigot, Mrs. Long, the Masters Parker, the Mayoress of Warrington. Mrs. Shacklady, Mrs. Shillcock, Miss Dolly Greenhalgh, Miss B. Bouchier, Mr. W. Jackson, Miss Hayes, the Infant School Children, the School Girls, the School Boys, Miss McGregor. Messrs. Vera Dairies, Leonard Davies, C. Plinston, Dr. Parker, W. H. Woodcock, .T. H. Clarke, Pilling, Grant, Mynekyrae,E. Wallington, W. Silcock,T. R.Westbrook,Mi.s Gronott,Mr. Tionchier( for Walter Milner), Mrs. Parker, Miss Maisie Fawcett, Mr. A. Fawcett. Miss Daisy Fawcett, Miss Mabel Timperley, Mr. Harry Graham, Miss May Vernon, Mrs. Davenport, Miss Ethel McTntyre, Mrs. Swinton, Mr. Harry Isherwood, Miss Faulkner, and Mr. Broady. A further meeting of the Tree Planting Committee was held on Tuesday evening when it was decided to have a semi-public tree planting day in Ellesmere and Fairfield roads on Saturday afternoon the Tith, com- mencing at 2 o'clock. it was also decided to plant a number of silver birches in Whitefleld-road. An announcement was made that Lady Greenall had given a further subscription of five guineas and would give one tree to every five given by others after Monday last.

div.head: CHEAPENING OF TRANSIT OF TRAFFIC THROUGH LIVERPOOL.
div.p: CHEAPENING OF TRANSIT OF TRAFFIC THROUGH LIVERPOOL.

We have been furnished with particulars of an agreement recently entered into between the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board and the Railway Companies who run into Liverpool with the object of cheapening the transit of traffic through that port. The object of the agreement is of such importance to the traders of this country, and its effects are likely to be sfer reaching,that we think it desirable to draw the attention of our read ers to it. Briefly, the terms of the agreement, are, that the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board will provide, as far as may be possible, rail siding accommodation at ship- ping berths,and also reception sidings for the working of.:i railway traffic on the dock estate. The railway corre-d panies will send their wagons loaded with export traffic, or empty for the conveyance of import traffic, to any berth where rail sidings are provided. The Dock Board will manipulate the full and empty trucks on the Estate and haul them from or to the railway stations. The loading, unloading, covering, uncovering, and labelling of the trucks will be performed by the Ship Owner or authorised master porter, but as between the Dock Board and the Railway Companies, these services will, for the purpose of the Agreement, be deemed to be per- formed on behalf of the Dock Board. For the terminal accommodation and services thereby saved to them, the Railway Companies will make the following allowances - out of the carriage rate either to the Dock Board or to the Shipowner or Master Porter direct if desired by the Dock Board : (a) On traffic in class A of the General Railway Classification (exclusive of coal, coke, and patent fuel, which are subject to special arrangement), 11. per ton. (b) On traffic in class B of the General Railway Classification. 4d. per ton, (c) On traffic in class C of the General Railwey Classification in consignments of not less than two tons from or to a particular place on the railways, and direct to or from a particular ship (no allowance to be made on smaller consign- ments). 9d. per ton excepting where 25 per cent. of the rate (less cartagel amounts to less than Dd. per ton, when the 25 per cent, will he allowed. (d) On traffic in classes 1 to 5 of the General Railway Classification in consignments of not less than two tons from or to a particular place on the railways and direct to or from a particular ship (no allowances to be made on similar con- signments). Is. per ton excepting where 25 per cent, of the rate (less cartage) amounts to less than Is. per ton, when the 25 per cent, will be allowed. (c) On traffic (in lots of not less than two tons) cha rued at rates including Collection and Delivery in Liverpool, an additional sum to be allowed, equal to the cartage drawback from time to tim e allowed by the Companies, when the collection or Delivery is performed by consignees or senders from or to the Companies' Stations, provided the allowance under what is known as the " ten ton arrangement "is limited to Bd, per ton, the !same.] as at Birkenhead and Manchester Docks. The effect of the arrangements will be the under- mentioned sayings : (1) Cartage as between Dock and Railway Station, the general charge for which is Is. 3d. per ton. (2) The amount allowed by the Railway Companies under the above scale, less : (a) The slight difference between the present cost of loading or unloading to or from cart at the Dock Quay and the future cost of loading or unloading from the railway wagon. The master porters, charges for wagon loading or unloading together with sheeting, may be expected to be somewhat heavier than for loading or unloading carts. (b) The cost of haulage in railway wagons between Docks and Station. This will be payable by the Shipowner or Trader to the Dock Board, who have for the present fixed the charge at sd.per ton. Thus on a consignment in class 1, the saving would be :—ls. 3d. cartage, plus Is. terminal allowance, less sd. haulage in truck. and (say) 3d. indreased cost of master porterage. The nett saving would therefore be Is. 7d. per ton. There are two itnportant limitations to the arrange- ments. The first is that at the present there are rails laid at only certain of the berths. At n number of others rails can be laid and as a result of negotiations which are at present going on between the Dock Board and the individual shipping firms, it is expected that several other berths will very shortly be so equipped. The second limitation is that the Agreement onl applies to traffic in direct transit to or from shippingil and does not extend to traffic stored in Liverpool. We are informed that within the last few days out of one ship alone over 3,000 bales of' cotton were dealt with under the new Agreement, and it was estimated 'jf that on this consignment alone a saving of upwards of £3O was effected.

' It appears obvious that a very marked step has been taken in connection with reducing the charges on traffic tbroug,h the port of Liverpool, and we are quite sure , that the traders of the country will appreciate this effort and hasten to take advantage of it.

PEACE SUNDAY. By general agreement the Sunday next before Chnstmas Day is observed each year by ministers and their churches as Peace Sunday. This year it will fall on December 24th. As in previous years, the Executive of the Peace Society are sending out invitations for its observance to all ministers in charge in the kingdom to some Sunday school teachers, local preachers and others, and to the Protestant pastors in France, making a total of nearly 40,000. Literature will be sent as usual. The committee of the Peace Society are also engaged in preparing for the forthcoming General Election, by arranging to have special questions put to candidates during the electoral campaign: and their desire is to have this done, if possible, in every con- stituency. Friends of Peace, and supporters of the Society, will hardly need reminding that these special operations involve considerable labour, and of necessity additional expense, and they are asked kindly to bear the Society in mind in apportioning their benefactions.

RUNCORN'S WeLTER SUPPLY. On Wednesday Colonel A. J. Hepper, R. E., an inspector of the Local Government Board, held an inquiry at the Runcorn Town Hall into an application of the Urban District Council for a provisional order to alter and amend the Runcorn Commissioners' Act, 1893, so as to enable them to obtain a supply of water from the Vyrnwy mains of Liverpool CorporAtion, and power them to borrow money to carry out the necessary work.—Mr. F. A. Lake, the law clerk said the present consumption in the water area was 340,000 gallons per day,and the well which now formed the source of supply had reached its limit. The water was most unsuitable for boilers and for manufactures, being extremely hard, and some of the largest consumers.at their own expense in order to save time, had commenced laying the new main, with the approval of the Council who wished to take over the conections they had to put in.—The appli- cation was supported by the Castner-liellner Electrol- ytic Alkali Company, the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany, and Messrs. Timmis, engineers, it was stated that the life of a boiler with Runcorn water was only four years, and in some instances canal water was used in preference. There was no opposition, and the inspector went to view the line of new mains. M. Alexis Lemanit, who was found on Sunday in a house in the Rue Cardinal Lemoine, Paris, by the side of his dead sweetheart, with two bullet wounds in his temple, succumbed to his injuries in hospital on Tuesday.
